nella.etymology: Articulated preposition formed by the fusion of Old Italian in la ('in the', < Classical Latin ĭn ĭllam), with assimilation of -nl- to -ll- and apheresis of initial i-.

nelle.etymology: Articulated preposition formed by the fusion of Old Italian in le ('in the', < Classical Latin ĭn ĭllās / ĭllae), with assimilation of -nl- to -ll- and apheresis of initial i-.

nello.etymology: Articulated preposition formed by the fusion of Old Italian in lo ('in the', < Classical Latin ĭn ĭllum), with assimilation of -nl- to -ll- and apheresis of initial i-.

history.meaning: in the, into the (masculine singular before vowel/s+consonant/z)

nemmeno.etymology: Univerbation of the phrase né meno ('nor less, not even'), formed from né ('neither, nor', < Classical Latin nĕc) + meno ('less', < Classical Latin mĭnus), with regular syntactic gemination of -m-.

nero.etymology: Continues Classical Latin nĭger, nĭgrum ('black, dark, sable'), with regular lowering of short ĭ to closed e and vocalization/loss of -g- before -r- (*nĕgru > nero).

nessuno.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *ne ipse ūnus ('not even one'), compound of Classical Latin nĕ(c) + ipse ('himself, very') + ūnus ('one'), with palatal assimilation of -ps- (> Old Italian neuno / nissuno / nessuno).

neve.etymology: Continues Latin nĭx, nĭvem ('snow'), from the accusative nĭvem with regular Romance development ĭ > closed /e/.

niente.etymology: Exact Latin source debated; Treccani notes several proposals—most prominently Vulgar Latin *nec gentem ('not a soul/person') or *ne inde—with medieval Tuscan variants neente and neiente.

nipote.etymology: Continues Classical Latin nĕpōs, nĕpōtem ('grandson, descendant; in Late Latin also nephew/niece'), from Proto-Indo-European *népōts, preserving both senses ('grandchild' and 'nephew/niece') in Italian.

no.etymology: Continues Latin nōn in stressed standalone position, whereas unstressed proclitic position before a verb preserved the final nasal as non.

noce.etymology: Continues Classical Latin nŭx, nŭcem ('walnut, nut; walnut tree'), with regular lowering of short Latin ŭ to closed o (feminine for the walnut fruit, masculine il noce for the tree and its timber).

noi.etymology: Continues Classical Latin nōs ('we, us'), with regular Italian vocalization of final -s in monosyllables to -i (compare voi < vōs, sei < sĕx).

noioso.etymology: Derived from noia ('annoyance, tedium, boredom', borrowed in the 13th century via Old Occitan enoja / noja from Late Latin inŏdĭa / phrase mihi in ŏdĭō est, 'it is hateful to me', from Classical Latin ŏdĭum, 'hatred, aversion') + the suffix -oso.

nome.etymology: Continues Classical Latin nōmen ('name, title, noun'), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁nómn̥ ('name'), with regular loss of final -n.

non.etymology: Continues Latin nōn (itself from Old Latin noenum, 'not one'). In Italian it stands directly before the verb phrase to negate a clause.

nonna.etymology: Continues Late Latin nŏnna ('revered elder woman, nun, grandmother'), an affectionate nursery reduplication.

nonno.etymology: Continues Late Latin nonnus (originally a respectful address to an elder or monk), which replaced classical avus as the everyday word for grandfather.

nono.etymology: Continues Classical Latin nōnus ('ninth', contracted from Old Latin *novenos, ordinal numeral derived from nŏvem, 'nine').

normale.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin normālis ('made according to the carpenter's square, right-angled, regular'), derived from norma ('carpenter's square, rule, pattern, standard').

history.meaning: carpenter's square, rule -> made according to rule, regular

nostro.etymology: Continues Classical Latin nŏster, nŏstrum ('our, ours'), derived from nōs ('we, us').

nota.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin nŏta ('mark, sign, written character, memorandum, critical mark'), related to nōscĕre ('to come to know', past participle nōtus); in medieval music, applied to a written musical sign or pitch.

notare.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin nŏtāre ('to mark, designate with a mark, observe, write down'), denominative verb from nŏta ('mark, sign').

history.meaning: mark, sign -> to mark, observe, take note

notizia.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin nōtĭtĭa ('being known, celebrity, acquaintance, knowledge, notion, list'), derived from nōtus ('known', past participle of nōscĕre); in Italian specialized as 'piece of news, information, notice'.

notte.etymology: Continues Classical Latin nŏx, nŏctem ('night'), from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts ('night'), with regular assimilation of the -ct- cluster to geminate -tt-.

nove.etymology: Continues Classical Latin nŏvem ('nine'), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥ ('nine'), with regular loss of final -m.

novellina.etymology: Feminine of novellino ('newly arrived, inexperienced, beginner', diminutive of novello < Classical Latin nŏvĕllus, 'new, young, fresh', itself a diminutive of nŏvus, 'new').

nudo.etymology: Continues Classical Latin nūdus ('naked, bare, uncovered, unadorned'), from Proto-Indo-European *nogʷódʰos ('naked').

numero.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin nŭmĕrus ('number, count, quantity, musical measure').

nuovo.etymology: Continues Classical Latin nŏvus, nŏvum ('new, young, fresh, recent'), from Proto-Indo-European *néwos, with regular Tuscan diphthongization of stressed short ŏ in an open syllable to uo.

o.etymology: Continues Classical Latin aut ('or'), with regular monophthongization of Latin au to o and loss of final -t before consonants (while retaining euphonic -d in od before vowels).

occhiale.etymology: Derived from occhio ('eye', < Latin oculus); plural gli occhiali ('eyeglasses') was coined in late-thirteenth-century Italy where wearable spectacles were first crafted.

occhiata.etymology: Derived within Italian from occhio ('eye', < Latin ŏcŭlus) + the suffix -ata, designating a 'quick look, glance, gaze'.

occhio.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin ŏclus, syncopated from Classical Latin ŏcŭlus ('eye', originally diminutive of *ŏkʷ-, 'eye'), with regular Tuscan evolution of intervocalic -cl- to geminate palatal -cchi- (/kkj/).

occupare.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin occŭpāre ('to seize, take possession of, fill up, employ'), compound of ob- ('over, against') + root of capĕre ('to take, seize').

history.meaning: to take possession of, seize, busy

occupato.etymology: Continues Classical Latin occŭpātus ('taken possession of, engaged, busy, employed'), past participle of occŭpāre ('to occupy, busy').

history.meaning: to take up, engage -> busy, engaged, occupied
busy, occupied, taken (of a seat or phone line)

odore.etymology: Continues Latin odōr, odōrem ('smell, scent, fragrance'), cognate with Greek ὄζω (ózō, 'to smell').

offrire.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *offerīre, regularized fourth-conjugation verb from Classical Latin offerre ('to bring before, present, offer', compound of ob- + ferre, 'to bear, bring'), with syncope of the unstressed vowel.

oggetto.etymology: Learned borrowing from Medieval/Scholastic Latin obiectum ('something thrown or placed before the mind or senses, object'), substantivized neuter past participle of Classical Latin obĭcĕre ('to throw before, present', from ob- + iacĕre).

oggi.etymology: Continues Classical Latin hŏdĭē ('today', contracted from hōc dĭē, 'on this day'), with regular loss of initial h- and Tuscan evolution of intervocalic -di- before a vowel to geminate palatal -ggi- (/ddʒ/).

ogni.etymology: Continues Classical Latin ŏmnis, ŏmnes ('all, every'), with regular assimilation/palatalization in proclitic position of -mn- before final -i (< -ēs) to -gn- (/ɲɲ/, Old Italian ogne > ogni).

oh.etymology: Primary vocalic interjection of surprise, wonder, pleasure, or appeal, continuing Classical Latin ō / oh.

ok.etymology: Twentieth-century international borrowing from American English O.K. / okay, used in spoken Italian as an informal check or agreement.

olio.etymology: Continues Latin ŏlĕum ('olive oil'), an ancient Mediterranean word borrowed alongside Greek ἔλαιον (élaion).

oliva.etymology: Continues Latin ŏlīva ('olive fruit; olive tree'), early borrowing from archaic Greek *ἐλαίϝα (*elaíwa).

oltre.etymology: Continues Classical Latin ŭltrā ('beyond, on the further side, more than'), with regular lowering of short Latin ŭ to closed o and change of final -a to -e (via Old Italian oltra / oltre, influenced by adverbs in -e).

ombra.etymology: Continues Latin ŭmbra ('shadow, shade'), with regular Tuscan opening of tonic short ŭ to closed /o/.

onesto.etymology: Continues Classical Latin hŏnĕstus ('regarded with honor, honorable, respectable, upright'), derived from hŏnos / hŏnor ('honor, esteem').

oplà.etymology: Expressive exclamation accompanying a jump, lift, or sudden nimble movement, borrowed from or parallel to French hop là! (from the interjection hop! + là, 'there!').

oppure.etymology: Univerbation formed within Italian from o ('or', < Classical Latin aut) + pure ('yet, also, even', < Latin pūrē), with regular syntactic gemination of -p-.

ora.etymology: Continues Classical Latin hōra ('hour, time of day, season'), borrowed from Ancient Greek ὥρα (hṓra, 'season, time of day, hour'); used both as the noun 'hour' and (by ellipsis of in questa ora) as the temporal adverb 'now'.

orario.etymology: Learned continuation of Medieval/Late Latin hōrārius ('pertaining to the hours', derived from Classical Latin hōra, 'hour'); substantivized in the masculine (l'orario) for 'timetable, schedule, working/opening hours'.

ordinare.etymology: Continues Latin ōrdĭnāre ('to set in rows, arrange, command'), built on ōrdō, ōrdĭnis ('row, order').

ordinato.etymology: Continues Classical Latin ōrdĭnātus ('arranged in rows, set in order, regular, orderly'), past participle of ōrdĭnāre ('to set in order, arrange, command', from ōrdō, ōrdĭnis, 'row, rank, order').

ordine.etymology: Continues Latin ōrdinem (accusative of ōrdō, 'row, arrangement, command'), originally a weaving term for threads in a loom.

orecchio.etymology: Continues Latin aurĭcŭla (diminutive of auris, 'ear') via masculine reshaping *aurĭcŭlum, with au- > o- and -cl- > -cchi-.

organizzare.etymology: Learned continuation of Medieval/Late Latin organĭzāre ('to furnish with organs, play the organ; arrange systematically'), from Ancient Greek ὀργανίζειν (organízein, derived from ὄργανον, órganon, 'instrument, tool, organ'), reinforced in modern senses by French organiser.

ormai.etymology: Univerbation of the adverbial phrase or mai (also omai, 'now more, by now'), formed from ora ('now', < Latin hōra) + mai ('ever, more', < Latin măgis).

history.meaning: by now, at this point, now

oro.etymology: Continues Classical Latin aurum ('gold'), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂é-h₂us-o- ('glowing dawn-colored metal'), with regular monophthongization of Latin au to open o.

orologiaio.etymology: Derived with agent suffix -aio (< Latin -ārius) from orologio ('clock, watch', < Latin hōrolŏgĭum < Greek ὡρολόγιον, 'hour-teller').

orologio.etymology: Continues Latin hōrologium (from Ancient Greek hōrológion, 'hour-teller', from hṓra 'hour' + légein 'to tell').

ospitalità.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin hospĭtālĭtās, hospĭtālĭtātem ('hospitality, friendliness to guests'), derived from hospĭtālis ('relating to a guest or host', from hospĕs, hospĭtis).

ospitare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin hospĭtārī ('to lodge as a guest'), denominative verb from hospĕs, hospĭtis ('host; guest, stranger'), shifting in Italian to the transitive sense 'to host, receive as a guest, accommodate'.

ospite.etymology: Continues Latin hospitem (accusative of hospes), which already denoted both partners of hospitality—the host who welcomes and the guest who is welcomed.

ottanta.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *octanta, contracted from Classical Latin octōgintā ('eighty', derived from octō, 'eight'), with regular assimilation of -ct- to -tt-.

ottava.etymology: Feminine substantivisation of ottavo (< Latin octāvus, 'eighth', from ŏctō, 'eight'), short for ottava corda or ottava nota.

ottimo.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin ŏptĭmus ('best, very good', irregular superlative of bŏnus, 'good', related to ops, 'power, resources'), with regular assimilation of -pt- to -tt-.

otto.etymology: Continues Classical Latin ŏctō ('eight'), from Proto-Indo-European *oḱtōw ('eight'), with regular assimilation of the -ct- cluster to geminate -tt-.

ottone.etymology: Derived from Old Italian latone ('brass', with rebracketing of initial l- as the definite article: l'otone > ottone), borrowed from Arabic لَاطُون (lāṭūn, 'copper, brass', itself from Turkish altun, 'gold, copper').

ovunque.etymology: Univerbation modeled on Classical Latin ŭbīcŭmque ('wherever'), formed in Old Italian from ove ('where', < Latin ŭbĭ) + unque ('ever', < Latin ŭnquam).

pacchetto.etymology: Diminutive of pacco ('package, parcel, bundle', borrowed via Dutch/Germanic *pak from Middle Low German or French paquet) formed with the suffix -etto.

pace.etymology: Continues Classical Latin pāx, pācem ('peace, treaty, tranquility, calm'), built on the Proto-Indo-European root *peh₂ǵ- ('to fasten, fix, agree upon a pact').

pagare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin pācāre ('to make peaceful, pacify, appease', derived from pāx, pācis, 'peace'), which in Late/Vulgar Latin commercial usage came to mean 'to appease or satisfy a creditor by settling a debt, pay'.

pagina.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin pāgĭna ('column of writing on a papyrus roll, leaf, page', originally 'trellis of vines fastened together', from pangĕre, 'to fasten, fix').

history.meaning: to fasten -> column of writing, page

pagnotta.etymology: Formed on pane ('bread', < Latin pānis) with diminutive/round-shape suffix -otta (*paniotta), denoting a single round loaf.

paio.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *pārium ('a pair of equal things'), substantivized neuter from Classical Latin pār, păris ('equal, matching; a pair', plural păria, preserved in the feminine plural le paia), with regular Tuscan reduction of -ri- to -i-.

palazzo.etymology: From Latin Palātium (the Palatine Hill in Rome, site of the imperial residences), broadening in Italian cities to mean any multi-storey masonry town building.

pane.etymology: Continues Latin pānem (accusative of pānis, 'bread'), shared with compagno ('companion', literally one who shares bread).

panico.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin pānĭcus, from Ancient Greek πανικός (panikós, 'of the god Pan', as in πανικὸς φόβος, panikòs phóbos, 'sudden groundless terror attributed to the woodland god Pan').

history.meaning: sudden terror caused by the god Pan

panino.etymology: Diminutive of pane ('bread', < Classical Latin pānis, pānem) formed with the suffix -ino, designating a small bread roll or a filled sandwich.

pannello.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *pannĕllus ('small piece of cloth, patch', diminutive of Classical Latin pannus, 'cloth, rag'), reinforced in architectural and carpentry senses ('wooden or metal panel') by Old French panel / French panneau.

history.meaning: piece of cloth -> small cloth, panel
piece of cloth, saddle pad, wooden panel

panno.etymology: Continues Classical Latin pannus ('piece of cloth, garment, rag, cloth wrap').

history.meaning: cloth, cleaning rag, woolen fabric; clothes (pl. panni)

paragrafo.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin parăgrăphus, from Ancient Greek παράγραφος (parágraphos, short for παράγραφος γραμμή, 'marginal stroke written beside a text to mark a break in sense or speaker', from παραγράφειν, 'to write beside').

history.meaning: marginal mark indicating a section break

parcheggiare.etymology: 20th-century denominative verb from parcheggio ('parking, parking lot'), adapted from English parking / to park (itself ultimately from Old French parc, 'enclosed ground where military vehicles and horses were stationed').

history.meaning: to leave a vehicle in a designated space

parete.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *parētem (with shift from -iĕ- to closed -ē-), from Classical Latin părĭēs, părĭĕtem ('wall of a room or house, partition wall', as opposed to mūrus, 'outer defensive/structural wall'), shifting from masculine to feminine gender.

parlare.etymology: Continues Christian Late Latin parabolāre ('to speak in parables, converse', from Greek parabolḗ), which became the everyday word for speaking in Italian and French.

parola.etymology: Continues Christian Late Latin parăbŏla ('comparison, parable, speech, word of Christ', borrowed from Ancient Greek παραβολή, parabolḗ, 'comparison, allegory'), which via syncopated Vulgar Latin *paraula (> parola) displaced Classical verbum across most of Romance.

parte.etymology: Continues Classical Latin pars, partem ('part, portion, share, side, direction, role').

partire.etymology: Continues Classical Latin partīrī / partīre ('to divide, share, distribute', derived from pars, partis, 'part'), which in Late/Vulgar Latin reflexive/intransitive usage (sē partīre ab, 'to separate oneself from') came to mean 'to depart, leave, set out'.

passare.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *passāre ('to take steps, walk through, cross, pass'), denominative verb derived from Classical Latin passus ('step, pace').

history.meaning: to pass, go by, spend (time), hand over

passo.etymology: Continues Classical Latin passus, passum ('step, stride, pace, footprint, mountain pass', originally 'stretching out of the legs in walking', from pandĕre, 'to spread, stretch out', past participle passus).

history.meaning: to stretch out -> stride, step, pace

pasta.etymology: Continues Late Latin pasta ('kneaded dough, paste'), from Greek πάστη (pástē, 'barley porridge, salted meal').

paura.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *pavōra, originally a collective neuter plural reshaped from Classical Latin păvor, păvōrem ('trembling, dread, fear, panic', derived from păvēre, 'to tremble with fear, be terrified'), with loss of intervocalic -v-.

pavimento.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin păvīmentum ('hard floor of rammed earth, stone, or mosaic tiles'), derived from păvīre ('to beat down, ram, tread flat').

history.meaning: to ram, beat flat -> rammed or tiled floor

pazienza.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin pătĭĕntĭa ('endurance, forbearance, patience'), derived from pătĭēns, present participle of pătī ('to suffer, bear, endure').

pedale.etymology: Continues Classical Latin pĕdālis ('of a foot, foot-long, pertaining to the foot', derived from pēs, pĕdis, 'foot'); substantivized in Italian (whence French pédale and English pedal) for an organ, piano, or bicycle 'foot lever, pedal'.

peggio.etymology: Continues Classical Latin pĕĭus ('worse', neuter comparative of mălus, 'bad', and comparative adverb of mălē, 'badly'), with regular Tuscan evolution of intervocalic -i- (/j/) to geminate palatal -ggi- (/ddʒ/).

pelle.etymology: Continues Classical Latin pĕllis, pĕllem ('animal hide, pelt, skin'), from Proto-Indo-European *pelnis ('skin, film').

penna.etymology: Continues Classical Latin pĕnna ('feather, wing; in Late Latin, quill pen for writing'), from Old Latin petna (< Proto-Indo-European *péth₂r̥ / *pet-neh₂, from *peth₂-, 'to fly').

pennellata.etymology: Derived within Italian from pennello ('paintbrush', < Classical Latin pēnĭcĭllum / pēnĭcĕllus, 'painter's brush, small tail', double diminutive of pēnis, 'tail') + the single-action suffix -ata.

pennello.etymology: Continues Latin pēnicĭllus ('small tail; painter's tuft brush'), double diminutive of pēnis ('tail').

pensare.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin pēnsāre ('to weigh carefully, ponder, consider', frequentative of pĕndĕre, 'to weigh'), whereas the inherited popular development yielded pesare ('to weigh').

history.meaning: to weigh -> to weigh in the mind, ponder

per.etymology: Continues Classical Latin pĕr ('through, by means of, during, for the sake of'), which in Italian absorbed the functions of Classical prō ('for, on behalf of, in exchange for').

history.meaning: for, through, by, in order to

perbacco.etymology: Univerbation of the mild euphemistic exclamation per Bacco! ('by Bacchus!', invoking the Roman god of wine Bacchus in place of sacred religious names).

perché.etymology: Univerbation of the phrase per che ('for what [reason/cause]', from per < Latin pĕr + che < Latin quid / quod), functioning as both 'why?' and 'because, so that'.

history.meaning: for what reason / for the reason that

perdere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin pĕrdĕre ('to destroy, ruin, waste, lose irrevocably'), compound of per- ('through, to destruction') + dăre / *-dĕre ('to put').

perfetto.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin pĕrfĕctus ('thoroughly made, completed, finished, accomplished, faultless'), past participle of pĕrfĭcĕre ('to bring to completion', from per- + facĕre, 'to make, do').

history.meaning: to complete thoroughly -> completed, flawless, perfect

perfino.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase per fino ('up to the end, even'), formed from per ('through, for') + fino ('until, up to', < Latin fīnis).

permesso.etymology: Continues Classical Latin pĕrmĭssus ('allowed, granted', past participle of pĕrmĭttĕre, and fourth-declension action noun pĕrmĭssus, 'leave, permission'); also used as a polite formula when entering a room or passing through ('excuse me, may I come in?').

history.meaning: to let through, allow -> allowed; permission
permission, permit; excuse me / may I come in?

permettere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin pĕrmĭttĕre ('to let pass through, give leave, allow, permit'), compound of per- ('through') + mĭttĕre ('to let go, send').

perno.etymology: Continues Latin pĕrna ('ham, leg, wooden tenon or pivot shaped like a haunch') via Vulgar Latin *pĕrnum.

persiana.etymology: Substantivized feminine of the adjective persiano ('Persian', < Latin Persiānus), modeled in the 18th century on French persienne ('louvered window shutter with slanted slats', so named because such ventilated blinds were associated with Persia and the Near East).

persino.etymology: Univerbation of Old Italian per sino ('even, right up to'), variant of perfino formed from per + sino ('up to, until', altered from fino by crossing with segno < Latin signum).

persona.etymology: Continues Classical Latin persōna ('actor's theatrical mask; dramatic character, role; legal person, individual human being'), probably borrowed into Latin from Etruscan φersu ('masked figure').

però.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin per hōc ('for this reason, therefore', compound of Classical Latin pĕr + ablative hōc); in Old Italian it meant 'therefore' (preserved in però che), before shifting through negative clauses to the adversative sense 'however, yet, but'.

pesante.etymology: Participial adjective from the present participle of pesare ('to weigh, be heavy', < Vulgar Latin *pēsāre < Classical pēnsāre).

pesare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin pēnsāre ('to weigh out, counterbalance', frequentative of pĕndĕre, 'to weigh'), with regular Vulgar Latin reduction of the -ns- cluster to -s- (*pēsāre; compare learned pensare, 'to think').

peso.etymology: Continues Classical Latin pēnsum ('portion of wool weighed out to a spinner for a day's work; weight', neuter past participle of pĕndĕre, 'to weigh'), with regular Vulgar Latin reduction of -ns- to -s- (*pēsum).

piacere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin plăcēre ('to please, be agreeable, be welcome'), with regular Tuscan palatalization of initial pl- to pi- (/pj/); substantivized in the masculine (il piacere) for 'pleasure, favor' and as the polite greeting 'pleased to meet you'.

history.meaning: to be pleasing, like (verb); pleasure, favor, nice to meet you (noun)

piacevole.etymology: Adjective formed in Old Italian from piacere ('to please', < Classical Latin plăcēre) + the suffix -evole (< Latin -ĭbĭlis), meaning 'pleasant, agreeable, enjoyable'.

pianerottolo.etymology: Derived within Tuscan from piano ('flat level, floor', < Latin plānus) with the interfix -er- and diminutive suffix -ottolo, designating the flat 'landing' at the top of a flight of stairs.

piangere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin plangĕre ('to strike, beat the breast in mourning, lament aloud'), with regular Tuscan palatalization of initial pl- to pi- (/pj/), which in Italian displaced Classical flēre ('to weep').

history.meaning: to beat the breast in grief, lament

piano.etymology: Continues Classical Latin plānus ('flat, level, even, clear, low-voiced'), with regular Tuscan palatalization of initial pl- to pi- (/pj/); used as an adjective ('flat, slow, soft'), adverb ('slowly, quietly'), and noun ('flat surface, story/floor of a building, plan', and by clipping from pianoforte, 'piano').

history.meaning: flat, slow, quiet; floor/story, plan, piano

pianoforte.etymology: Shortened from gravicembalo col piano e col forte ('harpsichord with soft and loud'), coined in Florence by Bartolomeo Cristofori around 1700 for his hammer-action keyboard instrument.

pianta.etymology: Continues Classical Latin planta ('sprout, shoot, cutting for propagation; sole of the foot'), with regular Tuscan evolution of initial pl- to pi- (/pj/), uniting the botanical sense ('plant') and the architectural/cartographic sense ('floor plan, map', originally the 'footprint' of a building).

history.meaning: plant shoot; sole of the foot
plant, tree; floor plan, map; sole of the foot

piantina.etymology: Diminutive of pianta ('plant; floor plan, map', < Classical Latin planta) formed with the suffix -ina, designating both a 'young seedling, small potted plant' and a 'floor plan, street map'.

history.meaning: small plant, seedling; floor plan, layout, map

piattino.etymology: Diminutive of piatto ('plate, dish', < Late Latin *plattus) formed with the suffix -ino, designating a small plate or teacup 'saucer'.

piatto.etymology: Continues Vulgar/Late Latin *plattus ('flat, level'), borrowed from Ancient Greek πλατύς (platýs, 'broad, flat'), with regular Tuscan palatalization of initial pl- to pi- (/pj/); substantivized in the masculine (il piatto) for a flat serving 'plate, dish, course of a meal'.

piazza.etymology: Continues Latin platĕa ('broad street, open courtyard'), borrowed from Greek πλατεῖα (plateîa, 'wide way'), with regular Italian development of -tj- > -zz- and pl- > pi-.

piazzetta.etymology: Diminutive of piazza ('public square, plaza', < Classical Latin plătĕa, 'broad street, courtyard', borrowed from Ancient Greek πλατεῖα [ὁδός], plateîa [hodós], 'broad way') formed with -etta.

piccolo.etymology: Formed from the expressive childish/sound-symbolic root *pikk- ('small, tiny point', compare piccino, pizzico, Spanish pequeño) with the unstressed diminutive suffix -olo (< Latin -ŭlus).

piede.etymology: Continues Latin pēs, pĕdem ('foot'), with regular Tuscan diphthongisation of stressed open ĕ in an open syllable (pĕde > piede).

piegare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin plĭcāre ('to fold, bend, roll up'), with regular Tuscan palatalization of initial pl- to pi- (/pj/), lowering of short ĭ to closed e, and voicing of intervocalic -c- to -g-.

pieghevole.etymology: Adjective derived from piegare ('to fold, bend', < Classical Latin plĭcāre) + the suffix -evole (< Latin -ĭbĭlis), meaning 'foldable, collapsible, pliable' (also substantivized for a folded 'brochure, leaflet').

pieno.etymology: Continues Classical Latin plēnus ('full, filled, complete'), from the Proto-Indo-European root *pleh₁- ('to fill'), with regular Tuscan palatalization of initial pl- to pi- (/pj/).

pietra.etymology: Continues Classical/Late Latin pĕtra ('rock, crag, stone'), borrowed from Ancient Greek πέτρα (pétra, 'rock, boulder'), which in Vulgar Latin displaced Classical lăpis, with regular Tuscan diphthongization of stressed short ĕ in an open syllable to ie.

pinzetta.etymology: Diminutive of pinza ('pincers, pliers, tongs', deverbal from pinzare, 'to pinch, nip, grip', of expressive origin *pints-* / reinforced by French pince and pincer) formed with -etta, designating 'tweezers, small tongs'.

history.meaning: to pinch, grip -> pliers, tongs -> tweezers, small tongs

pioggia.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *ploia for classical pluvia ('rain', from pluere, 'to rain'), with pl- > pi- and -vj- > -ddʒ-.

piolo.etymology: Tuscan derivative (via *pediŏlum) of Latin pĕdĭcŭlus / pēs ('little foot, support peg, rung').

piovere.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *plŏvĕre (shifted to the third conjugation from Classical Latin plŭĕre / archaic plŏvĕre, 'to rain'), with regular Tuscan palatalization of initial pl- to pi- (/pj/).

piovigginare.etymology: Frequentative/attenuative verb formed within Italian from piovere ('to rain', < Vulgar Latin *plŏvĕre) with the suffix -igginare (compare caliginare), meaning 'to drizzle, rain lightly'.

pizzico.etymology: Deverbal noun from pizzicare ('to pinch, nip, tingle, pluck a string'), formed on the expressive/sound-symbolic root *pīts- / *pikk- ('sharp point, pinch, beak').

pizzo.etymology: Built on the expressive root *pīts- ('sharp point, peak, tip', whence 'pointed beard/goatee' and mountain 'peak'); the textile sense 'lace' arises from the pointed scallops or зубцы (merletti a pizzo) along the edge of lace trim.

più.etymology: Continues Classical Latin plūs ('more'), with regular Tuscan palatalization of initial pl- to pi- (/pj/) and loss of final -s (triggering syntactic gemination of a following consonant).

placca.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th–18th centuries from French plaque ('metal plate, badge, slab'), derived from Middle Dutch placke ('flat disk, coin, patch, metal plate').

history.meaning: plate, wall switch cover, badge, plaque

poco.etymology: Continues Classical Latin paucus, paucum ('few, little'), with regular monophthongization of Latin au to open o.

history.meaning: little, a little, few, not much

poggiare.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *pŏdĭāre ('to ascend a hillock; to prop up, rest upon a pedestal or support', derived from Classical Latin pŏdĭum, 'elevated base, parapet, hillock', < Ancient Greek πόδιον, pódion), or apheretic form of appoggiare.

history.meaning: to rest upon a base, prop

poi.etymology: Continues Classical Latin pŏst ('after, behind, afterward') via Vulgar Latin *pŏs (before palatal/front sounds > poi).

polvere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin pŭlvis, pŭlvĕrem ('dust, powder, fine sand'), shifting in Italian from masculine to feminine gender, with regular lowering of short ŭ to closed o.

pomeriggio.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin pōmērīdĭum ('time after midday, afternoon', originally also the sacred strip of land behind the city wall), compound of post ('after') + mĕrīdĭēs ('midday, noon'), with regular Tuscan evolution of intervocalic -di- to -ggi- (/ddʒ/).

pomodoro.etymology: 16th-century compound of pomo d'oro ('golden apple'), naming the first yellow-fruited varieties brought from the Americas to Renaissance Italy.

ponte.etymology: Continues Latin pontem (accusative of pōns, 'bridge'), keeping masculine gender in Italian (il ponte).

porcellana.etymology: Originally the Old Italian name of the glossy cowrie shell (porcellana, from porcella, 'little sow'), extended by Marco Polo to translucent Chinese ceramic whose glaze resembled the shell.

porta.etymology: Continues Latin porta ('city gate, doorway'), from the Indo-European root *per- ('to pass through'), cognate with porto ('harbour') and English port.

portare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin pŏrtāre ('to carry, bear, convey, bring'), which in Vulgar Latin and Romance completely displaced ferre.

portone.etymology: Augmentative of porta ('door, gate', < Classical Latin pŏrta) formed with the suffix -one, designating the large main entrance door or carriage gate of an apartment building or palace.

history.meaning: large main entrance door, front building gate

postino.etymology: Derived within Italian from posta ('mail, postal service', from Medieval Latin pŏsĭta [stătĭō], 'fixed relay station where couriers changed horses', feminine past participle of pōnĕre) + the occupational suffix -ino.

posto.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin pŏstus, syncopated from Classical Latin pŏsĭtus ('placed, set, situated', past participle of pōnĕre, 'to put, place'), substantivized in the masculine (il posto) for 'place, spot, seat, job position'.

history.meaning: place, spot, seat, space, job; placed (participle)

potere.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *potēre, regularized from classical posse ('to be able', contraction of potis esse).

povero.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *paupĕrus (remodeled as a first/second-declension adjective from Classical Latin third-declension paupĕr, paupĕrem, 'producing little, poor, scanty', from paucus + parĕre), with monophthongization of au to open o.

pranzo.etymology: Continues Classical Latin prandĭum ('late-morning or midday meal, luncheon', from *prām-ed-iom, 'first eating'), reshaped in Tuscan via prandio / desinare or back-formed from pranzare (< *prandiāre), with evolution of -di- after -n- to the dental affricate -z-.

preciso.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin praecīsus ('cut off in front, shortened, brief, clear-cut, exact'), past participle of praecīdĕre ('to cut off in front, abridge', from prae- + caedĕre, 'to cut').

history.meaning: to cut off cleanly -> clear-cut, exact, precise

preferire.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin praeferre ('to carry in front, hold before, prefer', compound of prae- 'before' + ferre 'to bear, carry'), adapted to the fourth conjugation (-ire).

preferito.etymology: Participial adjective and noun from preferire ('to prefer', < Classical Latin praeferre), meaning 'favorite, preferred'.

pregare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin prĕcārī (Vulgar Latin active *prĕcāre, 'to ask earnestly, beg, entreat, pray', derived from prĕx, prĕcis, 'prayer, entreaty'), with regular voicing of intervocalic -c- to -g-.

history.meaning: to pray, beg, ask politely (ti prego)

prego.etymology: First-person singular of pregare ('to pray, ask earnestly'), from Latin precārī; shortened from vi/La prego ('I beg you / please do') into Italian's all-purpose courteous reply.

premere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin prĕmĕre ('to press, squeeze, push down, bear upon').

prendere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin prĕhĕndĕre / prēndĕre ('to lay hold of, grasp, seize, take', compound of prae- + *hendĕre, cognate with English get).

prenotare.etymology: Learned or administrative compound formed from Classical Latin praenŏtāre ('to mark beforehand, note down in advance', from prae- 'before' + nŏtāre 'to mark, record'), specialized in modern Italian for 'to book, reserve in advance'.

prenotazione.etymology: Action noun derived within Italian from prenotare ('to book, reserve in advance', < Latin praenŏtāre) + the suffix -zione (< Latin -tiō, -tiōnem).

preoccuparsi.etymology: Reflexive form of preoccupare, learned continuation of Classical Latin praeoccŭpāre ('to seize beforehand, occupy the mind in advance', from prae- + occŭpāre); in reflexive use, 'to worry, be anxious, take care of'.

history.meaning: to seize beforehand, engross the mind
to trouble -> to worry, be concerned

preparare.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin praepărāre ('to make ready beforehand, prepare, equip'), compound of prae- ('beforehand') + părāre ('to make ready, furnish').

pressione.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin prĕssĭō, prĕssĭōnem ('act of pressingdown, pressure, leverage'), derived from prĕmĕre ('to press', past participle prĕssus).

presto.etymology: Continues Late Latin praestus ('ready, at hand, prompt, quick'), adjectival back-formation from the Classical Latin adverb praestō ('at hand, ready, present', in praestō esse), used in Italian both as an adverb ('soon, early, quickly') and as an adjective ('quick, ready').

previsione.etymology: Learned formation from Late Latin praevīsĭō, praevīsĭōnem ('foreseeing, foresight'), derived from Classical Latin praevĭdēre ('to see beforehand, foresee', past participle praevīsus).

previsto.etymology: Past participle of prevedere ('to foresee, expect, provide for', < Classical Latin praevĭdēre, from prae- + vĭdēre), formed on the model of visto (past participle of vedere).

history.meaning: to foresee, expect -> foreseen, expected, scheduled

prezioso.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin prĕtĭōsus ('of great value, costly, precious'), derived from prĕtĭum ('price, worth, value').

prezzo.etymology: Continues Classical Latin prĕtĭum ('worth, value, price, reward'), with regular Tuscan evolution of postvocalic -ti- to geminate dental affricate -zz- (/tts/).

prima.etymology: Continues Classical Latin prīma (feminine singular or neuter plural of prīmus, 'first', originally in temporal phrases such as prīmā hōrā, 'at the first hour'), functioning as an adverb ('before, earlier, first') and noun ('first class/gear, premiere').

primavera.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *prīma vēra, from Classical Latin prīmō vēre ('at the start of spring', from prīmus 'first' and vēr 'spring').

primo.etymology: Continues Classical Latin prīmus ('first, foremost', superlative built on the prepositional root *pro- / prae-, 'before, in front').

principale.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin prīncĭpālis ('first, original, chief, principal'), derived from prīnceps, prīncĭpis ('first in order, chief, leader', from prīmus + capĕre).

privato.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin prīvātus ('apart from the state, belonging to an individual, personal, private', originally past participle of prīvāre, 'to set apart, deprive', from prīvus, 'single, one's own').

history.meaning: single, one's own -> to separate -> private, personal

problema.etymology: Learned borrowing from Classical Latin prŏblēma ('question proposed for academic discussion, riddle'), from Ancient Greek πρόβλημα (próblēma, 'something thrown forward, jutting obstacle, task or question put forward', from προβάλλειν, probállein).

professionista.etymology: Derived within Italian from professione ('profession, declared occupation', < Classical Latin prŏfĕssĭō, prŏfĕssĭōnem, 'public declaration [of one's occupation]', from prŏfĭtērī) + the suffix -ista.

profondo.etymology: Continues Classical Latin prŏfŭndus ('deep, bottomless, vast', compound of prō- + fŭndus, 'bottom'), with regular lowering of short Latin ŭ to closed o.

profumare.etymology: Formed from pro- (< Latin prō-) + fumare ('to smoke, emit vapor or scented fumes', < Classical Latin fūmāre, from fūmus, 'smoke, steam'), originally 'to scent by burning aromatic resins or incense'.

history.meaning: to scent with aromatic smoke -> to perfume, smell sweet

profumo.etymology: Deverbal noun from profumare ('to scent, perfume', from pro- + fumare, 'to emit scented smoke'); spread from Renaissance Italy (or Catalan/Occitan perfum) across Europe (French parfum, English perfume).

history.meaning: to scent with aromatic smoke, perfume

progettare.etymology: Denominative verb formed from progetto ('plan, design, project', borrowed via French projet from Classical Latin prōiectum, 'something thrown forward', neuter past participle of prōĭcĕre, from prō- + iacĕre).

progresso.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin prōgrĕssus ('a going forward, advance, progress'), action noun derived from prōgrĕdī ('to step forward, advance', from prō- + grădī, 'to step, walk').

promettere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin prōmĭttĕre ('to let go forward, send forth; to foretell, pledge, promise'), compound of prō- ('forth') + mĭttĕre ('to send').

promuovere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin prōmŏvēre ('to move forward, push onward, advance, promote'), compound of prō- + mŏvēre ('to move'), reshaped on the conjugation and diphthong of muovere.

pronto.etymology: Continues Classical Latin prōmptus ('brought forth, ready at hand, quick, prompt', past participle of prōmĕre, 'to take or bring out', from prō- + emĕre), with regular simplification of the three-consonant cluster -mpt- to -nt-; also used as the standard telephone greeting ('hello?, ready on the line').

history.meaning: to bring out -> ready at hand, prompt

proporzione.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin prōpōrtĭō, prōpōrtĭōnem ('comparative relation, symmetry, analogy, proportion', coined by Cicero from the phrase prō pōrtĭōne, 'in accordance with each part's share').

proprietario.etymology: Learned continuation of Late/Juridical Latin prŏprĭĕtārĭus ('owner of property'), derived from Classical Latin prŏprĭĕtās ('ownership, property', from prŏprĭus, 'one's own').

proprio.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin prŏprĭus ('one's own, special, particular, characteristic', possibly from prō prīvō, 'in a private capacity'); used both as an adjective ('own, proper') and as an emphatic adverb ('really, truly, right, exactly').

history.meaning: one's own (adj.); really, truly, right, just (adv.)

prossimo.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin prŏxĭmus ('nearest, next, immediately following or preceding', superlative formed from the root of prŏpĕ, 'near'), with regular assimilation of -x- to -ss-.

proteggere.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin prōtĕgĕre ('to cover in front, roof over, shield, protect'), compound of prō- ('in front') + tĕgĕre ('to cover, roof').

history.meaning: to cover in front, shield, protect

prova.etymology: Continues Late Latin prŏba ('test, trial, proof, inspection'), deverbal noun from Classical Latin prŏbāre ('to test, try, prove').

provare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin prŏbāre ('to test the goodness of something, try, examine, prove, approve', denominative from prŏbus, 'good, upright, sound'), with regular spirantization of intervocalic -b- to -v-.

history.meaning: sound, good -> to test, try, prove
to try, test, try on, rehearse, feel (an emotion)

prudere.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *prūdĕre, dissimilated and shifted to the third conjugation from Classical Latin prūrīre ('to itch, tingle, long for').

pubblico.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin pūblĭcus ('pertaining to the people or state, public, common', altered from Old Latin poplicus by crossing with pūbēs, 'adult population', from pŏpŭlus, 'people'), with regular Tuscan gemination of -bl- to -bbl-.

pulire.etymology: Continues Classical Latin pŏlīre ('to smooth, polish, furbish, make neat and bright'), with pretonic raising of o to u, shifting in Italian from 'to polish' to the general verb 'to clean'.

pulito.etymology: Continues Classical Latin pŏlītus ('smoothed, polished, neat, refined'), past participle of pŏlīre ('to smooth, polish, clean').

history.meaning: to polish, clean -> polished, neat, clean

puntare.etymology: Denominative verb from punta / punto ('point, tip', < Late Latin pŭncta / Classical pŭnctum, from pŭngĕre, 'to prick, pierce'), meaning 'to point, aim, prop, bet'.

history.meaning: point -> to aim, point at, stake/bet

punto.etymology: Continues Classical Latin pŭnctum ('small hole made by pricking, point, dot, spot, brief moment', substantivized neuter past participle of pŭngĕre, 'to prick, puncture'), with regular assimilation of -nct- to -nt- and lowering of short ŭ to closed o.

history.meaning: point, dot, period/full stop, stitch, score

puntualità.etymology: Derived from puntuale ('precise, on the dot, punctual', < Medieval Latin pŭnctuālis, derived from Classical Latin pŭnctum, 'point [in space or time]') + -ità.

pure.etymology: Continues Classical Latin pūrē ('purely, simply, merely, without qualification', adverb of pūrus, 'pure, clean'), which in Old Italian shifted from 'only, merely' to 'also, too, even, go ahead and...'.

history.meaning: also, too, even; please do / go ahead (with imperatives)

puro.etymology: Continues Classical Latin pūrus ('clean, unmixed, unstained, pure'), from the Proto-Indo-European root *pewh₂- ('to cleanse, purify').

purtroppo.etymology: Univerbation of the adverbial phrase pur troppo ('only too much, all too truly'), formed from pur(e) ('merely, only, indeed') + troppo ('too much'), shifting from 'only too much' to 'unfortunately, alas'.

qualche.etymology: Univerbation in Old Italian of qual che (sia) ('whatever [it may be]', from quale < Latin quālis + che < Latin quid; parallel to Old French quel que > quelque), developing the indefinite determiner sense 'some, a few, any'.

history.meaning: some, a few (followed by singular noun)

qualcosa.etymology: Univerbation of the phrase qualche cosa ('some thing'), formed from qualche ('some') + cosa ('thing', < Latin causa).

qualcuno.etymology: Univerbation of the phrase qualche uno ('some one'), formed from qualche ('some') + uno ('one', < Latin ūnus).

quale.etymology: Continues Classical Latin quālis, quālem ('of what sort, what kind of, which; such as'), built on the interrogative/relative stem *kʷo-.

quando.etymology: Continues Classical Latin quandō ('when, at what time; since'), temporal interrogative and relative adverb built on the stem *kʷo-.

quanto.etymology: Continues Classical Latin quantus, quantum ('how great, how much, pl. how many; as much as').

history.meaning: how much, how many, as much as
how much, how many, as much as

quaranta.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *quarranta, reduced from Classical Latin quadrāgintā ('forty', derived from quattuor, 'four').

quarantaquattro.etymology: Compound cardinal numeral formed within Italian from quaranta ('forty', < Vulgar Latin *quarranta < Classical quadrāgintā) + quattro ('four', < Classical Latin quattuor).

quartiere.etymology: Derived from quarto ('fourth part, quarter', < Latin quartus) + -iere (reinforced by Old French quartier), originally designating one of the four administrative or military divisions of a medieval city or camp.

history.meaning: fourth part of a town, district, military quarters

quarto.etymology: Continues Classical Latin quartus, quartum ('fourth; a fourth part, quarter'), ordinal numeral derived from quattuor ('four').

quasi.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin quăsĭ ('as if, just as, bijna, almost, nearly', from quam + sī).

quassù.etymology: Univerbation of the adverbial phrase qua su ('here up, up here'), formed from qua ('here', < Latin eccu(m) hāc) + su ('up', < Old Italian suso < Latin sūrsum), with regular syntactic gemination of -s-.

quattordici.etymology: Continues Classical Latin quattuōrdĕcim ('fourteen', compound of quattuor 'four' + dĕcem 'ten'), with final -i on analogy with dodici, tredici, quindici.

quattro.etymology: Continues Classical Latin quattuor ('four'), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwóres ('four'), with metathesis/remodeling of the final syllable to -tro.

quello.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *(ec)cu(m) ĭllum ('behold that one over there'), compound of Classical Latin eccum ('behold!') + distal demonstrative ĭlle, ĭllum ('that').

quercia.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *quĕrcĕa (substantivized feminine of the Classical Latin adjective quĕrcĕus, 'of oak', derived from quĕrcus, 'oak tree'), which replaced fourth-declension feminine quĕrcus.

questo.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *(ec)cu(m) ĭstum ('behold this one here'), compound of Classical Latin eccum ('behold!') + proximal demonstrative ĭste, ĭstum ('this [of yours / near us]').

qui.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *(ec)cu(m) hīc ('behold here'), parallel to qua from *(ec)cu(m) hāc.

quiete.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin quĭēs, quĭētem ('rest, repose, stillness, calm, peace'), from the Proto-Indo-European root *kʷyeh₁- ('to rest, be quiet').

quindi.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *(ec)cu(m) ĭnde ('from there, thence, after that'), formed from Classical Latin eccum + ĭnde ('thence, from there'), evolving from a spatial/temporal sense ('from there, next') to a logical connective ('therefore, so, then').

quindici.etymology: Continues Classical Latin quīndĕcim ('fifteen', compound of quīnque 'five' + dĕcem 'ten'), with final -i on analogy with dodici, tredici, quattordici.

raccomandata.etymology: Elliptical substantivization of lettera raccomandata ('registered letter'), feminine past participle of raccomandare ('to entrust to someone's care, recommend, register', formed from ri- + accomandare < Late Latin accommandāre, from ad- + commendāre).

raccontare.etymology: Formed from ri- + accontare ('to reckon up, relate, tell', from a- + contare < Classical Latin compŭtāre, 'to reckon, recount', reinforced by Old French reconter / raconter).

raddrizzare.etymology: Reinforced compound formed within Italian from ri- + a- + drizzare / dirizzare ('to make straight, set upright', < Vulgar Latin *dīrēctiāre, built on Classical Latin dīrēctus, 'straight'), with syntactic gemination of -d-.

history.meaning: to straighten up, set right again

raffreddare.etymology: Reinforced parasynthetic verb formed within Italian from ri- + a- + freddo ('cold', < Vulgar Latin *frĭgdu < Classical frīgĭdus) + -are, with syntactic gemination of -f-, meaning 'to cool down, make cold'.

ragazzo.etymology: Attested in medieval Italy first in the sense 'stable-boy, groom, servant lad'; widely traced to Maghrebi/Andalusian Arabic رَقَّاص (raqqāṣ, 'courier, messenger boy, runner'), which passed into medieval maritime and customs administration before generalizing to 'boy, youth'.

raggiante.etymology: Participial adjective from the present participle of raggiare ('to beam, radiate rays of light', denominative from raggio < Classical Latin rădĭus, 'spoke of a wheel, beam, ray').

ragione.etymology: Continues Classical Latin rătĭō, rătĭōnem ('reckoning, account, calculation; faculty of reason, motive, right', derived from rērī, 'to reckon, think', past participle rătus), via Old French raison or northern/Tuscan palatalization of intervocalic -ti- to -gi- (/ʒ/ > /dʒ/).

rame.etymology: Continues Late/Vulgar Latin *aerāmen ('copper, bronze, bronze vessels', derived from Classical Latin aes, aeris, 'copper ore, bronze', replacing aes across Romance; compare French airain).

ramo.etymology: Continues Latin rāmus ('tree branch, bough'), from the accusative rāmum.

rampicante.etymology: Participial adjective and noun from the present participle of rampicare ('to climb, clamber, creep up a support', derived from rampa / rampare, of Germanic origin *rampa, 'hook, claw, paw').

history.meaning: to climb -> climbing plant, creeper, vine

rapido.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin răpĭdus ('tearing away, rushing, swift, rapid'), derived from răpĕre ('to seize, snatch, carry off swiftly').

history.meaning: to snatch, sweep along -> swift, rapid

re.etymology: Continues Classical Latin rēx ('king'), reduced in Italian (either from the nominative rēx or by apocope of Old Italian rege < accusative rēgem) to the monosyllable re.

history.meaning: king; re, D (second note of the musical scale, from Resonare fibris)

realtà.etymology: Learned borrowing from Medieval/Scholastic Latin rĕālĭtās, rĕālĭtātem ('actual existence, reality'), coined from Late Latin rĕālis ('relating to things themselves, real', from Classical Latin rēs, 'thing, fact').

recensione.etymology: Learned borrowing from Classical Latin rĕcēnsĭō, rĕcēnsĭōnem ('official enumeration, revisión, assessment'), derived from rĕcēnsēre ('to count over, examine carefully, review', from re- + cēnsēre); acquired its modern sense 'critical review of a book or performance' in the 19th century via German Rezension.

history.meaning: review (of a book, film, or service), critical edition

reception.etymology: Unadapted 20th-century international hospitality borrowing from English reception / French réception ('hotel front desk'), ultimately from Classical Latin rĕcĕptĭō, rĕcĕptĭōnem ('act of receiving or welcoming', from rĕcĭpĕre).

registrato.etymology: Participial adjective from registrare ('to enter in a register, record, adjust/tune'), derived from Medieval Latin rĕgĭstrāre (built on Late Latin rĕgĕsta, 'things recorded').

history.meaning: to enter into a register, record
to record, adjust -> recorded, registered, adjusted

registro.etymology: Continues Medieval Latin rĕgĭstrum (with epenthetic -r-), from Late Latin rĕgĕstum / plural rĕgĕsta ('list, catalog, things transcribed or recorded'), substantivized neuter past participle of Classical Latin rĕgĕrĕre ('to carry back, enter into a record book', from re- + gĕrĕre).

history.meaning: to transcribe back -> recorded items, register
register, logbook, attendance book, vocal/musical register

regola.etymology: Semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin rēgŭla ('straight wooden ruler, measuring rod; pattern, rule, standard'), derived from rĕgĕre ('to keep straight, guide, rule').

history.meaning: to guide straight -> straightedge, rule, principle

regolamento.etymology: Derived within Italian from regolare ('to regulate, govern by rules', < Late Latin rēgŭlāre, from rēgŭla, 'rule') + the suffix -mento, designating a formal set of rules or bylaws.

history.meaning: to direct according to a rule

rendere.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *rĕndĕre, remodeled with a nasal infix (on the analogy of its antonym prēndĕre, 'to take') from Classical Latin rĕddĕre ('to give back, return, yield, render', compound of red- + dăre, 'to give').

history.meaning: to return, give back, yield, make (render)

respirare.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin rĕspīrāre ('to breathe out, fetch one's breath, breathe'), compound of re- ('back, again') + spīrāre ('to blow, breathe').

history.meaning: to breathe back and forth, breathe

respiro.etymology: Deverbal noun from respirare ('to breathe', < Classical Latin rĕspīrāre), meaning 'breath, breathing, respite'.

responsabile.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via French responsable (or directly formed in legal Latin), derived from Classical Latin rĕspōnsus (past participle of rĕspŏndēre, 'to answer for, promise in return, be answerable').

history.meaning: to answer for, be legally answerable
responsible, in charge; manager, person in charge (noun)

restare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin rĕstāre ('to stand back, stay behind, remain, be left over'), compound of re- ('back, behind') + stāre ('to stand, stay').

resto.etymology: Deverbal noun from restare ('to remain, be left over', < Classical Latin rĕstāre), designating 'the remainder, rest' and in commerce 'change (money returned)'.

retro.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin rĕtrō ('backward, behind, at the back'), used in Italian as a prefix and substantivized masculine noun ('back, rear, reverse side').

riapertura.etymology: Formed within Italian from the iterative prefix ri- ('again', < Latin re-) + apertura ('opening', < Classical Latin apertūra).

riaprire.etymology: Formed within Italian from the iterative prefix ri- ('again', < Latin re-) + aprire ('to open', < Classical Latin aperīre).

riavvitare.etymology: Formed within Italian from the iterative prefix ri- ('back, again', < Latin re-) + avvitare ('to screw in, fasten with screws', parasynthetic verb from a- + vite, 'screw').

history.meaning: to screw back on, screw in again

ricambio.etymology: Deverbal noun from ricambiare ('to exchange in return, replace', from ri- + cambiare < Late Latin cambiāre), specialized in phrases like pezzo di ricambio for a 'spare part, replacement'.

history.meaning: replacement, spare part, return (of a favor/greeting)

ricco.etymology: Borrowed in the early Middle Ages from Germanic (Lombardic *rīhhi or Gothic reiks, 'powerful, mighty, wealthy', from Proto-Germanic *rīkijaz, itself an ancient borrowing from Celtic *rīg-, 'king').

ricevuta.etymology: Substantivized feminine past participle of ricevere ('to receive', < Classical Latin rĕcĭpĕre, 'to take back, receive'), originally in elliptical commercial phrases such as (quietanza / cedola) ricevuta ('acknowledgment of sum received, receipt').

riconoscere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin rĕcognōscĕre ('to know again, recall to mind, examine, recognize'), compound of re- ('again') + cognōscĕre ('to get to know, know').

ricordare.etymology: Continues Late/Classical Latin rĕcŏrdārī (Vulgar Latin active *rĕcŏrdāre, 'to call back to mind, remember, recollect'), compound of re- ('back, again') + cŏr, cŏrdis ('heart', regarded in antiquity as the seat of memory).

history.meaning: heart -> to bring back to heart/mind, remember

ricordo.etymology: Deverbal noun from ricordare ('to remember, recall', < Latin rĕcŏrdārī), designating a 'memory, recollection, keepsake, souvenir'.

riempire.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *rĕimplīre (shifted to the fourth conjugation from Classical Latin rĕimplēre, 'to fill up again', compound of re- + implēre, 'to fill').

history.meaning: to fill -> to fill up again

riga.etymology: Borrowed in the early Middle Ages from Germanic (Lombardic) *rīga ('line, row, furrow, streak', cognate with Old High German rīga and Middle Dutch rīge).

righello.etymology: Diminutive of riga ('straightedge, line', < Lombardic *rīga) formed with the masculine suffix -ello, designating a desk 'ruler' for drawing straight lines and measuring.

rimanere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin rĕmănēre ('to stay behind, abide, remain, endure'), compound of re- ('behind') + mănēre ('to stay, dwell, remain').

rimboccare.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed from ri- + in- (assimilated to im- before b) + bocca ('mouth, opening, brim', < Latin bŭcca), originally 'to turn back the mouth or top edge of a sack or sheet', hence 'to tuck in (bedsheets), roll up (sleeves)'.

history.meaning: to fold back the edge/brim, roll up (sleeves), tuck in (sheets)

rimettere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin rĕmĭttĕre ('to send back, slacken, forgive'), recomposed in Italian with the sense of mettere ('to put, place') as 'to put back, replace, postpone, lose (money)'.

rimpatriata.etymology: Substantivized feminine past participle of rimpatriare ('to return to one's homeland', from ri- + in- + patria, 'fatherland, home'), used colloquially for a 'happy reunion or get-together of old friends'.

history.meaning: to return home -> homecoming; joyful reunion of old friends

ringraziare.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed within Italian from ri- + in- + grazia ('grace, favor, pl. thanks', < Classical Latin grātĭa) + -are, meaning 'to give thanks, thank'.

rintocco.etymology: Deverbal noun from rintoccare ('to toll again, strike the hours on a bell'), formed from ri- + in- + toccare ('to touch, strike a bell', of onomatopoeic origin *tokk-*).

history.meaning: tolling, chime, stroke of a bell

riparare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin rĕpărāre ('to get ready again, restore, renew, repair', compound of re- + părāre, 'to prepare, furnish'), also merging in Italian with Late Latin *rĭpărĭāre ('to protect with a bank/rampart, shelter').

history.meaning: to repair, fix, mend; to shelter, protect

riparazione.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Late Latin rĕpărātĭō, rĕpărātĭōnem ('restoration, renewal, repair'), derived from Classical Latin rĕpărāre ('to restore, repair').

ripetere.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin rĕpĕtĕre ('to seek again, return to, recommence, say or do over again'), compound of re- ('again') + pĕtĕre ('to seek, aim at').

history.meaning: to seek or do again, repeat

riportare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin rĕpŏrtāre ('to carry back, bring back, report'), compound of re- ('back, again') + pŏrtāre ('to carry, bring').

history.meaning: to bring back, return, report, carry over

riposare.etymology: Continues Late Latin rĕpausāre ('to pause again, take rest, repose'), compound of re- + Late Latin pausāre ('to halt, cease, rest', derived from pausa < Ancient Greek παῦσις, paûsis, 'cessation, stop').

history.meaning: to pause, cease -> to rest, repose

ripostiglio.etymology: Derived within Italian from riposto ('put away, stored out of sight', past participle of riporre < Classical Latin rĕpōnĕre, 'to put back, lay up, store away') + the locative/diminutive suffix -iglio (< Latin -ĭcŭlum).

riprendere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin rĕprĕhĕndĕre / rĕprēndĕre ('to catch hold of again, hold back, rebuke'), recomposed in Italian with the senses of prendere ('to take') as 'to take back, resume, scold, film/shoot'.

history.meaning: to take back, resume, recover, film

riquadro.etymology: Deverbal noun from riquadrare ('to square off, divide into square or rectangular panels'), formed from ri- + quadro ('square', < Classical Latin quadrum, from quattuor, 'four').

history.meaning: to square off, frame -> square panel, inset box, pane

riscaldamento.etymology: Action noun derived within Italian from riscaldare ('to heat up, warm', from ri- + scaldare < Late Latin excaldāre, 'to wash in hot water, heat', from calĭdus / caldus, 'hot') + -mento.

riserva.etymology: Deverbal noun from riservare ('to keep back, save for later use, reserve'), which continues Classical Latin rĕsĕrvāre (compound of re- 'back' + sĕrvāre 'to keep safe, preserve').

history.meaning: to reserve -> reserve, backup supply, reservation

rispettare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin rĕspĕctāre ('to look back at repeatedly, have regard for, respect'), frequentative of rĕspĭcĕre (or denominative from rispetto).

history.meaning: to look back at -> to regard, respect

rispetto.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin rĕspĕctus ('a looking back, regard, consideration, respect'), action noun derived from rĕspĭcĕre ('to look back at, consider', from re- + spĕcĕre, 'to look').

history.meaning: to look back at, consider -> regard, consideration, respect

rispondere.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *rĕspŏndĕre, shifted to the third conjugation from Classical Latin rĕspŏndēre ('to promise in return, answer, reply', compound of re- + spŏndēre, 'to pledge solemnly').

risveglio.etymology: Deverbal noun from risvegliare ('to wake up, reawaken'), formed from ri- + svegliare ('to awaken', < Vulgar Latin *exvĭgĭlāre, from Classical Latin ēvĭgĭlāre / vĭgĭlāre, 'to be awake, watch', via Old Occitan esvelhar).

history.meaning: to wake up, rouse from sleep

ritardo.etymology: Deverbal noun from ritardare ('to delay, slow down, be late', < Classical Latin rĕtardāre, compound of re- + tardāre, from tardus, 'slow, late').

ritmo.etymology: Continues Latin rhythmus, from Greek ῥυθμός (rhythmós, 'measured flow, cadence, proportion'), related to ῥέω ('to flow').

ritrovare.etymology: Formed within Italian from the iterative prefix ri- ('again', < Latin re-) + trovare ('to find', < Vulgar Latin *trŏpāre, 'to compose, invent, find').

history.meaning: to find again, rediscover, meet up

riuscire.etymology: Compound formed within Italian from ri- ('again, out') + uscire ('to go out, come out', < Classical Latin exīre), evolving from 'to come out again, emerge at a result' to 'to turn out well, succeed, manage to'.

history.meaning: to come out, turn out -> to succeed, manage to

rivolgere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin rĕvŏlvĕre ('to roll back, turn over, unwind', compound of re- + vŏlvĕre), reshaped on the palatalized stem of volgere ('to turn, direct').

rivolto.etymology: Participial adjective from rivolgere ('to turn toward, direct', < Classical Latin rĕvŏlvĕre, modeled on volto < vŏlūtus), meaning 'turned toward, facing, directed at' (and as a noun, 'lapel, cuff, chord inversion').

rompere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin rŭmpĕre ('to break, burst, shatter, tear asunder'), with regular lowering of short Latin ŭ to closed o.

ronzare.etymology: Onomatopoeic verb (*rondz-*, imitating the continuous buzzing or humming sound of bees, flies, or electrical machinery).

rosso.etymology: Continues Classical Latin rŭssus ('red, reddish', cognate with rŭber and rūfus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rewdʰ-s-o-s), with regular lowering of short Latin ŭ to closed o.

rotolo.etymology: Continues Late Latin rŏtŭlus ('little wheel, scroll, roll'), diminutive of Latin rŏta ('wheel').

rotondo.etymology: Continues Classical Latin rŏtŭndus ('wheel-shaped, round, circular, spherical'), derived from rŏta ('wheel'), with regular lowering of short ŭ to closed o.

rotto.etymology: Continues Classical Latin rŭptus ('broken, burst, shattered'), past participle of rŭmpĕre ('to break'), with regular assimilation of -pt- to -tt- and lowering of short ŭ to closed o.

rovesciare.etymology: Denominative verb from rovescio ('reverse side, upside-down', continuing Vulgar Latin *rĕvĕrsĭus, extended from Classical Latin rĕvĕrsus, 'turned back, reversed', past participle of rĕvĕrtĕre), with regular Tuscan palatalization of -si- to -sci-.

history.meaning: to turn back -> turned backward, inside out
reverse, upside-down -> to spill, overturn, turn inside out

rubinetto.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th century from French robinet ('water tap, stopcock'), originally a diminutive of the medieval French proper name Robin (a pet form of Robert given in folklore to the ram, Robin le mouton, because early metal spigots and taps were cast in the shape of a ram's head).

history.meaning: pet name for a ram -> ram-headed tap, faucet

rumore.etymology: Continues Classical Latin rūmor, rūmōrem ('murmur, vague sound, hearsay, popular report'), with dissimilation/shortening of pretonic ū to u.

rumoroso.etymology: Adjective derived within Italian from rumore ('noise', < Classical Latin rūmor, rūmōrem) + the suffix -oso (< Latin -ōsus), meaning 'noisy, loud'.

ruota.etymology: Continues Classical Latin rŏta ('wheel'), from Proto-Indo-European *róth₂eh₂ ('wheel', from *reth₂-, 'to run, roll'), with regular Tuscan diphthongization of stressed short ŏ in an open syllable to uo.

sabato.etymology: Continues Christian Latin sabbătum, borrowed via Greek σάββατον (sábbaton) from Hebrew šabbāth ('day of rest', from šābath, 'to cease from work').

sacchetto.etymology: Diminutive of sacco ('sack, bag', < Classical Latin saccus < Ancient Greek σάκκος, sákkos, of Semitic origin: Hebrew/Phoenician śaq, 'coarse haircloth sack') formed with the suffix -etto.

saggio.etymology: Confluence of two distinct etyma: (1) as 'wise, prudent' (and 'wise person'), via Old French sage / Old Occitan savi from Vulgar Latin *săpĭus (derived from săpĕre, 'to have taste, be wise'); (2) as 'test, sample, assay, essay', continuing Late Latin exăgĭum ('weighing, balance, trial weight', from exĭgĕre).

sala.etymology: Borrowed in the early Middle Ages from Germanic (Lombardic) *sala ('single-room hall, great hall of a manor, reception room', from Proto-Germanic *saliz, 'hall, dwelling').

history.meaning: hall, large room, dining/living room, auditorium

salato.etymology: Continues Classical/Late Latin sălātus ('salted, seasoned with salt'), participial adjective from *sălāre / sălīre (derived from sāl, sălis, 'salt'); figuratively 'steep, expensive' (of a bill or price).

sale.etymology: Continues Latin sāl, sălem ('salt'), pan-Indo-European root *séh₂ls shared with English salt and German Salz.

salire.etymology: Continues Classical Latin sălīre ('to leap, jump, bound, mount'), which in Italian shifted from 'to leap up' to the general verb 'to go up, climb, ascend' (while its frequentative saltāre took over the sense 'to jump').

history.meaning: to go up, climb, get on (a vehicle)

saltare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin saltāre ('to dance, leap repeatedly, bound'), frequentative of sălīre ('to leap, jump'), taking over the primary sense 'to jump, leap, skip'.

history.meaning: to leap -> to leap repeatedly, dance, jump
to jump, leap, skip, blow (of a fuse)

salutare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin sălūtāre ('to wish health to, greet, salute, pay one's respects'), denominative verb from sălūs, sălūtis ('health, safety, welfare, greeting').

history.meaning: health, welfare -> to wish health to, greet
to greet, say hello/goodbye to, wave to

salvare.etymology: Continues Late Latin salvāre ('to make safe, rescue, save, deliver'), denominative verb from Classical Latin salvus ('safe, unharmed, whole'), which in Christian Latin replaced Classical servāre in the sense 'to save'.

salve.etymology: Learned continuation of the Classical Latin greeting formula salvē! ('be well!, hail!, hello!', second-person singular imperative of salvēre, 'to be in good health', from salvus, 'safe, well').

history.meaning: to be well -> be well!, hail!, hello!

salvo.etymology: Continues Classical Latin salvus ('safe, unharmed, whole, sound'), from Proto-Indo-European *solh₂wós ('whole, intact'); also used prepositionally (from ablative absolute formulae like salvō iūre) to mean 'except, save for, unless'.

sano.etymology: Continues Classical Latin sānus ('sound in body or mind, healthy, whole, uninjured').

santo.etymology: Continues Classical Latin sānctus ('made sacred, consecrated, inviolable, holy', originally past participle of sancīre, 'to consecrate, ratify solemnly'), with regular simplification of the -nct- cluster to -nt-.

sapere.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *săpēre, shifted to the second conjugation from Classical Latin săpĕre ('to have a taste or flavor; to have discernment, be wise, understand'), which across Romance displaced Classical scīre in the sense 'to know (a fact or how to do something)'.

history.meaning: to taste of; to be discerning, know
to know, know how to; to taste/smell of (sapere di)

sapone.etymology: Continues Classical/Late Latin sāpō, sāpōnem ('mixture of tallow and ashes used by Gauls and Germans to tint hair and wash, soap'), an early Latin borrowing from Proto-Germanic *saipǭ ('resin, soap').

sapore.etymology: Continues Classical Latin săpor, săpōrem ('taste, flavor, relish, discernment'), derived from săpĕre ('to taste, have flavor').

satinato.etymology: Participial adjective from satinare ('to give a smooth, matte or satin finish to paper, glass, or metal'), borrowed in the 19th century from French satiner (derived from satin, 'satin silk', via Medieval Latin/Spanish aceituní from Arabic زَيْتُونِيّ, zaytūniyy, 'of Zaytun [Quanzhou, China]').

history.meaning: satin -> to give a satin finish

sbagliare.etymology: Formed with the intensive/privative prefix s- (< Latin ex-) + abbagliare ('to dazzle, blind momentarily, cause to mistake', built on bagliore / *balĭare), shifting from 'to be dazzled in vision' to 'to make a mistake, err, get wrong'.

sbagliato.etymology: Participial adjective from sbagliare ('to make a mistake, get wrong'), meaning 'wrong, mistaken, incorrect'.

history.meaning: to make a mistake, get wrong

sbaglio.etymology: Deverbal noun from sbagliare ('to make a mistake, err'), meaning 'mistake, error, blunder'.

sbattere.etymology: Formed with the intensive prefix s- (< Latin ex- / dis-) + battere ('to beat, strike', < Vulgar Latin *battĕre < Classical battuĕre), meaning 'to slam, bang, beat, whisk (eggs)'.

sbirciare.etymology: Denominative verb formed with the prefix s- (< Latin ex-) + bircio ('squinting, bleary-eyed, short-sighted', of expressive or uncertain dialectal origin), meaning 'to peer at sidelong, peek, glance furtively'.

history.meaning: to peek at, glance sidelong, peer

scaffale.etymology: Probably derived from Medieval Latin *scapha / Lombardic *skafa ('wooden tub, shelf, board'), originally designating an open set of wooden shelves for books or wares.

scala.etymology: Continues Latin scāla ('ladder, flight of steps'), related to scandere ('to climb'); used in Italian for stairs, ladders, and musical scales.

scaldare.etymology: Continues Late Latin excaldāre ('to bathe or wash in hot water, warm up'), parasynthetic verb formed from ex- + Classical Latin calĭdus / syncopated caldus ('warm, hot').

history.meaning: to wash in hot water, heat

scambiare.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *excambiāre ('to exchange, trade, swap'), compound of ex- + Late Latin cambiāre ('to barter, exchange', of Gaulish origin).

history.meaning: to exchange, swap, mistake one thing for another

scambio.etymology: Deverbal noun from scambiare ('to exchange, swap', < Vulgar Latin *excambiāre), designating an 'exchange, trade, swap' or a railway 'track switch'.

history.meaning: to swap -> exchange, trade, railway switch

scappare.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *excappāre ('to slip out of one's cloak [leaving it in the pursuer's hands], flee, escape'), parasynthetic verb formed from ex- ('out of') + Late Latin cappa ('hooded cloak, cape').

history.meaning: cloak -> to slip out of one's cloak and flee
to run away, escape, slip out

scaricare.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *excarricāre ('to unload a cart or burden'), formed from the privative prefix ex- + Late Latin carrĭcāre ('to load on a wagon', from carrus, 'four-wheeled wagon').

history.meaning: to unload, dump, drain, run down (a battery), download

scarpa.etymology: Attested in northern and Tuscan Italian from the 13th–14th centuries; generally derived from Germanic (Lombardic or Gothic) *skarpō ('sharp-pointed leather pouch or footwear', from Proto-Germanic *skarpaz, 'sharp, pointed').

history.meaning: sharp, pointed -> pointed shoe or pouch

scatola.etymology: Continues Medieval Latin castŭla / *catŭla (by metathesis of c-st to sc-t), borrowed from Frankish or Lombardic *kasto ('chest, box, coffer', cognate with Old High German kasto and German Kasten).

scavalcare.etymology: Formed with the privative/translocative prefix s- (< Latin ex-) + cavalcare ('to ride on horseback, straddle', < Late Latin caballĭcāre, from caballus, 'horse'), evolving from 'to unhorse, dismount' to 'to step or climb over (by throwing a leg across), bypass'.

history.meaning: to unhorse -> to climb over, step over, bypass

scegliere.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *exēlĭgĕre ('to pick out, select'), reinforced compound of ex- ('out') + Classical Latin ēlĭgĕre ('to pick out, choose', itself from ex- + lĕgĕre), with regular Tuscan palatalization of initial ex-e- to sce- (/ʃe/).

scelta.etymology: Substantivized feminine past participle of scegliere ('to choose, select', < Vulgar Latin *exēlĭgĕre, past participle scelto < *exēlĕctus).

scendere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin dēscĕndĕre ('to climb down, come down, descend', compound of dē- + scandĕre, 'to climb'), with apheresis of the initial syllable dē- and palatalization of sc- before e.

history.meaning: to go down, come down, get off (a vehicle)

scheggiarsi.etymology: Reflexive form of scheggiare ('to splinter, chip'), denominative verb from scheggia ('splinter, wood chip, shard', continuing Vulgar Latin *schĭdĭa < Classical Latin schĭdĭa, borrowed from Ancient Greek σχίδια, skhídia, 'wood splinters', from σχίζειν, skhízein, 'to split').

schermo.etymology: Deverbal noun from Old Italian schermire ('to defend, shield, fence'), borrowed from Lombardic *skirmjan ('to protect with a shield, defend', from Proto-Germanic *skirmijaną); evolved from 'protective barrier, fire-screen' to 'projection/television/computer screen'.

scherzo.etymology: Deverbal noun from scherzare ('to jest, play, frolic'), borrowed in the early Middle Ages from Lombardic *skërtsōn ('to leap about merrily, jest, sport', cognate with Middle High German scherzen and German Scherz).

history.meaning: to joke, play -> joke, prank, musical scherzo

schizzare.etymology: Confluence of two roots: (1) in the sense 'to splash, spurt, gush, dash off', of onomatopoeic origin (*skits-*, imitating a sudden liquid spurt); (2) in the artistic sense 'to sketch rapidly', denominal from schizzo ('rough sketch', < Classical Latin schĕdĭus, 'improvised, made extempore', < Ancient Greek σχέδιος, skhédios).

history.meaning: sound of spurting liquid / extempore sketch
to splash, spurt, squirt; to sketch

sciogliere.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *excolligĕre ('to untie, unbind, separate out from a bundle', formed from ex- + Classical Latin colligĕre, 'to gather, bind together', crossed with solvĕre, 'to loosen, untie, dissolve').

scivolare.etymology: Attested in Tuscan as an alteration of older/dialectal sifolare / zufolare (< Classical Latin sībĭlāre / *sīfĭlāre, 'to whistle, hiss, glide with a swishing sound') crossed with expressive roots for sliding (*skiv-*).

scolpire.etymology: Continues Classical Latin scŭlpĕre ('to carve in stone, wood, or metal, chisel, sculpt'), shifted to the fourth conjugation (-ire) with regular lowering of short ŭ to closed o.

sconosciuto.etymology: Participial adjective formed with the negative prefix s- (< Latin ex- / dis-) + conosciuto ('known', past participle of conoscere < Classical Latin cognōscĕre), meaning 'unknown, unfamiliar; stranger'.

scontato.etymology: Participial adjective from scontare ('to deduct from an account or bill, discount; to pay the penalty for', formed from s- < Latin ex- + contare < Late Latin compŭtāre, 'to reckon, count'); figuratively 'taken for granted, predictable'.

history.meaning: to deduct from a bill -> discounted, on sale; taken for granted

sconto.etymology: Deverbal noun from scontare ('to deduct from a bill or account', from s- + contare < Late Latin compŭtāre); exported from medieval and Renaissance Italian banking across Europe (French escompte, English discount).

history.meaning: to deduct from a sum or account

scontrino.etymology: Diminutive of scontro ('counter-tally, check-stub used to verify a payment or deposit', deverbal from scontrare, 'to match against a counter-register', from s- + contra) formed with -ino, designating a 'cash-register receipt, ticket stub'.

history.meaning: to match/verify -> tally, check -> sales receipt, claim stub

scorrere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin excŭrrĕre ('to run out, run forth, flow, hasten', compound of ex- + cŭrrĕre, 'to run'), with regular reduction of initial ex- before c- to s- and lowering of short ŭ to closed o.

history.meaning: to flow, glide, slide, skim through

scorso.etymology: Continues Classical Latin excŭrsus ('run through, elapsed, past', past participle of excŭrrĕre > scorrere, 'to flow, pass by in time').

history.meaning: to run out, pass by -> elapsed, past
to pass by -> last, past (e.g., la settimana scorsa)

scrittura.etymology: Continues Classical Latin scrīptūra ('writing, act or style of writing, written text or contract'), derived from scrībĕre ('to write', past participle scrīptus), with regular assimilation of -pt- to -tt-.

history.meaning: to write -> writing, written document, scripture

scrivania.etymology: Derived from Medieval Latin scrībānīa ('office or desk of a scribe/notary', from Late Latin scrībānum / scrība, 'public scribe, clerk', built on Classical scrībĕre, 'to write'), specialized for a 'writing desk'.

scrivere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin scrībĕre ('to scratch, engrave, draw lines, write with a stylus'), with regular spirantization of intervocalic -b- to -v-.

scuola.etymology: Continues Classical/Late Latin schŏla ('leisure given to learning, philosophical lecture, school'), borrowed from Ancient Greek σχολή (skholḗ, 'leisure, spare time, learned discussion, school'), with regular Tuscan diphthongization of stressed short ŏ to uo.

scuro.etymology: Continues Classical Latin ŏbscūrus ('dark, dim, shady, indistinct'), with apheresis of the unstressed initial syllable ob- (while learned oscuro preserves it).

scusa.etymology: Deverbal noun from scusare ('to excuse, pardon', apheretic form of escusare < Classical Latin excūsāre, 'to release from a charge or blame, plead in excuse', compound of ex- + causa, 'legal case, accusation').
