history.meaning: to free from a charge, excuse
to excuse -> excuse, apology (pl. scuse); sorry! / excuse me! (imperative)

scusare.etymology: Continues Latin excūsāre ('to release from a charge, excuse', from ex- + causa), losing unstressed initial ex- > s-.

se.etymology: Confluence of two Classical Latin words: (1) as the conditional and interrogative conjunction ('if, whether'), from Classical Latin sī via Vulgar Latin *sē (crossed with quid/quam); (2) as the stressed third-person reflexive pronoun (sé, 'himself, herself, oneself', and unstressed variant se before lo/la/li/le/ne), from Classical Latin sē.

secchio.etymology: Masculine back-formation beside secchia, continuing Late Latin sĭtŭla ('water bucket, well pail') via syncopated Vulgar Latin *sĭcla.

secco.etymology: Continues Classical Latin sĭccus ('dry, parched, thirsty, arid'), with regular lowering of short Latin ĭ to closed e.

secondo.etymology: Continues Classical Latin sĕcŭndus ('following, next in order, second; favorable', originally gerundive/participial adjective of sĕquī, 'to follow'); as a unit of time, from Medieval Latin pars minūta secunda ('second small division [of an hour]', i.e. 1/60 of a minute).

history.meaning: second (num. and noun); second course; according to (prep.)

sede.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin sēdēs, sēdem ('seat, chair, dwelling-place, abode, center'), built on the lengthened-grade root of sĕdēre ('to sit').

history.meaning: headquarters, seat, main office, venue, location

sedere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin sĕdēre ('to sit, remain seated'), from the Proto-Indo-European root *sed- ('to sit'); substantivized in the masculine (il sedere) as a colloquial/polite word for 'bottom, buttocks'.

history.meaning: to sit, be seated; bottom, seat (noun)

sedia.etymology: Derived within Italian from sedere ('to sit', < Latin sedēre), naming a backed chair.

sedici.etymology: Continues Classical Latin sēdĕcim ('sixteen', compound of sĕx 'six' + dĕcem 'ten'), with final -i on analogy with dodici, tredici, quattordici, quindici.

sedile.etymology: Continues Classical Latin sĕdīle ('seat, bench, stool, chair'), derived from sĕdēre ('to sit') with the instrument/place suffix -īle.

history.meaning: seat (in a car, train, theater, or park bench)

seduto.etymology: Participial adjective formed within Italian from sedere ('to sit', < Classical Latin sĕdēre) with the regular participial ending -uto (< Vulgar Latin *-ūtus), meaning 'seated, sitting down'.

segnalare.etymology: Denominative verb from segnale ('signal, sign, road sign', < Late/Medieval Latin sĭgnāle, substantivized neuter of Classical Latin sĭgnālis, 'serving as a sign', from sĭgnum), meaning 'to signal, report, point out'.

history.meaning: signal, sign -> to signal, point out, report

segnare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin sĭgnāre ('to set a mark upon, mark out, seal, indicate'), denominative verb from sĭgnum ('mark, sign'), with regular lowering of short ĭ to closed e and palatalization of -gn- (/ɲɲ/).

history.meaning: mark, sign -> to mark, seal, note
to mark, write down, score (a goal/point), indicate

segno.etymology: Continues Classical Latin sĭgnum ('identifying mark, token, sign, military standard, seal, constellation'), with regular lowering of short Latin ĭ to closed e and palatalization of -gn- (/ɲɲ/).

segreto.etymology: Continues Classical Latin sēcrētus ('set apart, separate, hidden, private, secret', past participle of sēcĕrnĕre, 'to sever, set apart', from sē- 'apart' + cĕrnĕre 'to sift, separate'), with popular voicing of intervocalic -cr- to -gr-.

history.meaning: to set apart -> hidden, private; secret

seguire.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *sĕquīre, regularized as an active fourth-conjugation verb from Classical Latin deponent sĕquī ('to follow, come after, pursue'), with voicing of intervocalic -qu- to -gu-.

history.meaning: to follow, attend, keep up with

sei.etymology: Continues Classical Latin sĕx ('six'), with regular Italian vocalization of final -x (/ks/) in monosyllables to -i (sĕx > *sĕs > sei); homophonous with sei ('you are', second-person singular present indicative of essere).

sembrare.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th century via Old Occitan semblar / Old French sembler ('to be like, seem, appear'), which continues Late Latin sĭmĭlāre ('to resemble, be like', derived from Classical Latin sĭmĭlis, 'like, similar'), with syncope and epenthetic -b- in the -m'l- cluster.

semplice.etymology: Continues Classical Latin sĭmplĕx, sĭmplĭcem ('single, uncompounded, plain, simple, frank', built on *sem- 'one' + *plek- 'to fold', literally 'single-fold'), with regular lowering of short ĭ to closed e.

semplicemente.etymology: Adverb formed from the adjective semplice ('simple, plain', < Classical Latin sĭmplĕx, sĭmplĭcem) + the adverbial suffix -mente (< Latin ablative mente).

sempre.etymology: Continues Classical Latin sĕmpĕr ('always, ever, at all times', built on *sem- 'one, together' + -per), with regular Tuscan metathesis/vowel-final adjustment of final -er to -re (compare quattro < quattuor).

sentimentalismo.etymology: Derived in the 19th century from sentimentale ('sentimental', borrowed via French sentimental from English sentimental, coined in the mid-18th century and popularized by Laurence Sterne's A Sentimental Journey, from sentiment < Medieval Latin sentīmentum, from sentīre, 'to feel') + -ismo.

sentire.etymology: Continues Classical Latin sĕntīre ('to perceive with the senses, feel, hear, think, experience'), which in Italian also became the everyday verb for 'to hear, listen to, taste, smell' alongside udire.

history.meaning: to perceive by the senses, feel
to feel, hear, listen to, taste, smell

senza.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *absentĭā, ablative of Classical Latin absentĭa ('in the absence of', derived from absēns, present participle of abesse, 'to be away'), with apheresis of the initial syllable ab- (Old Italian sanza / senza).

sera.etymology: From Latin sēra (diēs), feminine of sērus ('late'), naming the late hours of the day as daylight fades.

serata.etymology: Derived within Italian from sera ('evening', < Vulgar Latin *(hōra) sēra, feminine of Classical Latin sērus, 'late') + the duration/event suffix -ata (whence also French soirée).

serranda.etymology: Substantivized feminine gerundive formed within Italian from serrare ('to shut tightly, lock, close', < Late/Vulgar Latin *serrāre, from Classical Latin sĕra, 'door-bar, bolt', crossed with serra, 'saw'), designating a rolling metal 'shop shutter' or 'damper/flue valve'.

history.meaning: to close tightly -> rolling metal shutter, damper

serratura.etymology: Derived from serrare ('to lock, bolt, shut tightly', < Late/Vulgar Latin *serrāre, from Classical Latin sĕra, 'bolt, bar') + the instrument/result suffix -tura (< Latin -tūra).

servire.etymology: Continues Classical Latin sĕrvīre ('to be a servant or slave, serve, be useful to, wait upon'), denominative verb from sĕrvus ('slave, servant').

history.meaning: servant -> to serve, be of use to
to serve, be needed, be useful

servizio.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin sĕrvĭtĭum ('condition of a servant, service, attendance'), derived from sĕrvus ('servant') / sĕrvīre ('to serve').

history.meaning: service, duty, set of tableware, report

sette.etymology: Continues Classical Latin sĕptĕm ('seven'), from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥ ('seven'), with regular assimilation of -pt- to geminate -tt- and loss of final -m.

settimana.etymology: Continues Late Latin septimāna ('period of seven days'), derived from septem ('seven').

severo.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin sĕvērus ('serious, grave, strict, austere, stern').

sfidare.etymology: Continues Vulgar/Medieval Latin *exfīdāre ('to renounce one's feudal trust or allegiance, declare hostility, challenge to combat'), parasynthetic verb formed from privative ex- + fīdus / fīdēs ('trust, faith, allegiance').

sfilare.etymology: Formed within Italian from the prefix s- (< Latin ex-, either privative 'to unthread' or intensive 'to move in a line') + filo ('thread; row, line', < Classical Latin fīlum) / filare, meaning both 'to unthread, slip off, pull out' and 'to parade, march in a line'.

history.meaning: to unthread, slip off; to march in file, parade on a runway

sfornare.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed within Italian from the privative/extractive prefix s- ('out of', < Latin ex-) + forno ('oven', < Classical Latin fŭrnus) + -are (antonym of infornare), meaning 'to take out of the oven, turn out freshly baked'.

history.meaning: to take out of the oven, bake and turn out

sgabello.etymology: Continues Latin scabĕllum / scamĭllum ('low footstool, step bench'), diminutive related to scamnum ('bench'), with voicing of sc- > sg-.

si.etymology: Continues Classical Latin sē / dative sĭbĭ ('himself, herself, itself, themselves'), reduced in unstressed clitic position with raising of e to i to form the third-person reflexive, reciprocal, passive, and impersonal pronoun ('oneself, each other, one/people'); as the seventh note of the musical scale (B), formed from the initials of Sancte Ioannes in Guido of Arezzo's hymn Ut queant laxis.

history.meaning: oneself, each other, one (impersonal); si, B (musical note)

sicuramente.etymology: Adverb formed from the feminine adjective sicura ('safe, sure, certain', < Classical Latin sēcūrus) + the adverbial suffix -mente (< Latin ablative mente).

sicurezza.etymology: Abstract noun derived within Italian from sicuro ('safe, secure, sure', < Classical Latin sēcūrus) + the suffix -ezza (< Vulgar Latin *-ĭtia), meaning 'safety, security, certainty, confidence'.

sicuro.etymology: Continues Classical Latin sēcūrus ('free from care, untroubled, safe, confident, sure', compound of sē- 'without, apart from' + cūra 'care, anxiety'), with regular Tuscan raising of unstressed protonic e to i.

significare.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin sĭgnĭfĭcāre ('to show by signs, point out, indicate, mean, signify'), compound of sĭgnum ('sign, mark') + facĕre ('to make').

history.meaning: to make a sign, indicate, mean

signora.etymology: Feminine of signore ('lord, gentleman, Mr.', < Classical Latin sĕnĭor, sĕnĭōrem, 'older, elder'), formed with the feminine ending -a to mean 'lady, madam, Mrs., wife'.

signore.etymology: Continues Classical Latin sĕnĭor, sĕnĭōrem ('older, elder', comparative of sĕnĕx, 'old, old man'), which in Late Latin and feudal Europe became a title of authority and respect ('elder, lord, master, gentleman, Mr., the Lord').

history.meaning: gentleman, lord, Mr., Sir, the Lord

silenzio.etymology: Learned and popular continuation of Latin silentium ('silence, stillness'), from silēre ('to be silent').

silenzioso.etymology: Learned continuation of Late Latin sĭlĕntĭōsus ('full of silence, very quiet, still'), derived from Classical Latin sĭlĕntĭum ('silence, stillness', from sĭlēre, 'to be silent').

history.meaning: to be silent -> silence -> silent, quiet

sinceramente.etymology: Adverb formed from the feminine adjective sincera ('sincere, genuine', < Classical Latin sĭncērus) + the adverbial suffix -mente (< Latin ablative mente).

sincerità.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin sĭncērĭtās, sĭncērĭtātem ('soundness, purity, integrity, candor'), derived from sĭncērus ('pure, genuine, sincere').

sincero.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin sĭncērus ('clean, pure, unmixed, whole, genuine, candid', from Proto-Indo-European *sm̥-ḱerh₃-o-, literally 'of one growth, unmixed', from *sem- 'one' + root of crēscĕre).

singolo.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin sĭngŭlus (mostly plural sĭngŭlī, 'one each, one by one, individual, single, separate', built on the root *sem- 'one').

history.meaning: one at a time, individual, single

sinistra.etymology: Continues Classical Latin sĭnĭstra (feminine of sĭnĭster, with mănus 'hand' or pars 'side' understood), meaning 'left hand, left side'.

sinistro.etymology: Continues Classical Latin sĭnĭster, sĭnĭstrum ('on the left hand, left; in augury, unlucky/ominous'), preserving both the spatial sense 'left' and the figurative sense 'ominous, sinister; accident/claim'.

history.meaning: left (adj.); ominous, sinister (adj.); accident, insurance claim (noun)

sistemare.etymology: Denominative verb formed within Italian from sistema ('system, orderly arrangement', learned borrowing from Late Latin systēma < Ancient Greek σύστημα, sýstēma, 'organized whole, assembly', from συνιστάναι, 'to set together'), meaning 'to put in order, tidy up, arrange, fix, settle'.

history.meaning: system, order -> to tidy up, arrange, fix, settle

smarrire.etymology: Parasynthetic/intensive verb formed from the prefix s- (< Latin ex-) + Old Italian marrire ('to go astray, lose one's way, be bewildered'), borrowed from Frankish or Gothic *marrjan ('to hinder, lead astray, confuse').

history.meaning: to go astray, lose one's way
to misplace, lose, lose one's way

smettere.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *exmittere ('to send away, dismiss, cease'), formed from the privative/separative prefix ex- (> Italian s-) + mittere ('to send, let go, put').

history.meaning: to send away, leave off, stop

socia.etymology: Feminine form of socio, continuing Classical Latin socia ('female companion, partner, ally, associate'), feminine of socius.

socio.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin socius ('companion, comrade, ally, business partner'), from Proto-Indo-European *sokʷ-yo- ('follower, companion'), a derivative of the root *sekʷ- ('to follow'; compare Latin sequī).

sodo.etymology: Inherited popular continuation of Classical Latin solidum (accusative of solidus, 'solid, firm, compact, dense'), via syncopated Late Latin soldus with Tuscan loss of pre-dental -l- (compare the doublet soldo and the learned borrowing solido).

soffiare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin sufflāre ('to blow up from below, inflate, puff'), compound of sub- ('under, up from beneath') + flāre ('to blow'), with regular evolution of the cluster -ffl- to -ffi-.

soffio.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from soffiare ('to blow, puff'), which continues Classical Latin sufflāre ('to blow, inflate').

soffitta.etymology: Substantivized feminine past participle of Old Italian soffiggere ('to fasten beneath'), continuing Vulgar Latin *suffīcta (remodeled for Classical Latin suffīxa, feminine of suffīxus, past participle of suffīgere, 'to fasten underneath'), originally designating the planked structure under the roof and hence an attic or garret.

history.meaning: to fasten underneath, affix from below

soffitto.etymology: Substantivized masculine past participle of Old Italian soffiggere ('to fasten underneath'), continuing Vulgar Latin *suffīctum (remodeled after fīctus for Classical Latin suffīxum, past participle of suffīgere, 'to fasten from below', from sub- + fīgere), referring to planks fastened beneath the floor beams to form a ceiling.

history.meaning: to fasten underneath, nail from below

soglia.etymology: Continues Late and Vulgar Latin solia ('threshold, sill'), arising from a blend of Classical Latin solea ('sandal, sole, foundation timber, sill') and the neuter plural solia of solium ('seat, throne, threshold'), with regular palatalization of -lj- to -gli-.

sognare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin somniāre ('to dream, daydream'), denominative verb derived from somnium ('dream'), with regular development of -mnj- to palatal -gn-.

sogno.etymology: Continues Classical Latin somnium ('dream, vision'), derivative of somnus ('sleep'), with regular evolution of the cluster -mnj- to palatal nasal -gn- (/ɲɲ/).

sol.etymology: As the name of the fifth musical note of the scale (G), coined in the 11th century by Guido d'Arezzo from the initial syllable of solve polluti labii reatum ('absolve the guilt of a polluted lip'), the fifth hemistich of the Latin hymn Ut queant laxis; as a poetic or apocopated noun meaning 'sun', shortened from sole (< Classical Latin sōlem).

history.meaning: absolve (syllable from the hymn Ut queant laxis)
sol, G (musical note); sun (apocopated form of sole)

soldo.etymology: Continues Late Latin solidum (accusative of solidus [nummus], the imperial gold coin introduced by Constantine the Great, from Classical Latin solidus, 'solid, whole, massive'), via the syncopated form soldus; in the plural soldi, generalized to mean 'money'.

sole.etymology: Continues Classical Latin sōlem (accusative of sōl, 'sun'), from Proto-Indo-European *sóh₂wl̥ ('sun').

soleggiato.etymology: Participial adjective from soleggiare ('to shine, expose to the sun'), formed within Italian from sole ('sun', < Latin sōlem) + the verbal suffix -eggiare (< Late Latin -idiāre).

history.meaning: sun -> to expose to the sun -> sunny, sunlit

solido.etymology: Learned borrowing from Classical Latin solidus ('firm, dense, compact, whole, three-dimensional'), from Proto-Indo-European *solh₂- ('whole, well-kept'); a learned doublet of the inherited forms sodo and soldo.

solito.etymology: Continues Classical Latin solitum (accusative of solitus, 'accustomed, usual, habitual'), originally the past participle of the semi-deponent verb solēre ('to be accustomed, be wont').

sollevare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin sublevāre ('to lift up from beneath, raise, support, lighten, console'), compound of sub- ('under, up from below') + levāre ('to lighten, raise', derived from levis, 'light in weight'), with assimilation of -bl- to -ll-.

history.meaning: to lift up from below, support, relieve

sollievo.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from sollevare ('to lift up, relieve', < Classical Latin sublevāre), showing regular Tuscan diphthongization of stressed short open e (lĕv-) to -liev- in an open syllable.

solo.etymology: The adjective continues Latin sōlus ('alone, single'), while the adverbial sense 'only, just' continues Latin sōlum.

sonno.etymology: Continues Classical Latin somnum (accusative of somnus, 'sleep, slumber'), from Proto-Indo-European *swépnos ('sleep', from *swep-, 'to sleep'), with regular regressive assimilation of the cluster -mn- to -nn-.

sopra.etymology: Continues Classical Latin suprā ('above, over, on the upper side, beyond'), originally an ablative feminine singular form (suprā [parte]) of superus ('upper, higher', from super, 'over, above').

sopraluce.etymology: Compound formed within Italian from sopra- ('above, over', < Classical Latin suprā) + luce ('light, window opening', < Classical Latin lūcem), designating a small window or transom set above a door or main window to admit light.

soprattutto.etymology: Univerbation of the phrase sopra tutto ('above all, over everything'), composed of sopra ('above, over', < Classical Latin suprā) + tutto ('all, everything', < Late/Vulgar Latin *tōttus for Classical tōtus), with syntactic gemination of initial t- after sopra.

sorridere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin subrīdēre ('to smile, laugh slightly'), compound of sub- ('under, slightly, quietly') + rīdēre ('to laugh'), shifted to the third conjugation (*subrīdĕre) in Vulgar Latin as with ridere, with assimilation of -br- to -rr-.

sorriso.etymology: Continues Late/Vulgar Latin *subrīsum (from the Classical Latin past participle stem subrīs- of subrīdēre, 'to smile'), or substantivized from the past participle sorriso of sorridere.

sorso.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *sŭrsum ('a sip, swallow'), a participial noun remodeled from Classical Latin sorptum (past participle of sorbēre, 'to suck in, sip, swallow', perfect sorpsī), influenced by morsus ('bite').

sottile.etymology: Continues Classical Latin subtīlem (accusative of subtīlis, 'fine, thin, slender, delicate, acute'), originally a weaving term from sub- ('under') + tēla ('web, warp', i.e. thread passing beneath the warp), with regular assimilation of -bt- to -tt-.

sotto.etymology: Continues Classical Latin subtus ('below, beneath, underneath'), adverbial formation derived from the preposition sub ('under'), with regular assimilation of -bt- to -tt-.

spaccare.etymology: Borrowed from Lombardic *spahhan ('to split, cleave, crack'; compare Middle High German spachen, 'to split, burst'), from Proto-Germanic *spak-.

spalla.etymology: Continues Late Latin spatula ('shoulder blade, shoulder', originally a diminutive of Classical Latin spatha, 'broad flat wooden blade, paddle, spatula', < Ancient Greek spáthē), via syncopated Vulgar Latin *spatla with assimilation of -tl- to -ll-.

spartito.etymology: Substantivized masculine past participle of spartire ('to divide, distribute into parts'), from Vulgar Latin *expartīre (from ex- + Classical Latin partīrī, 'to divide, share', derived from pars, partis, 'part'), designating a musical composition written out and divided across staves.

history.meaning: to divide into parts -> musical score, sheet music

spavento.etymology: Deverbal noun from spaventare ('to frighten, terrify'), which continues Vulgar Latin *expaventāre, an intensive verb built on the present participle expavēns, expaventis of Classical Latin expavēre ('to be terrified at, dread', from ex- + pavēre, 'to tremble with fear').

spazio.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin spatium ('room, area, distance, expanse, interval of time').

spazzare.etymology: Continues Late and Vulgar Latin *spatiāre (active counterpart of Classical Latin spatiārī, 'to walk about, cover a space', derived from spatium, 'open space'), which developed the transitive meaning 'to make space, clear an area, sweep clean'.

history.meaning: space -> to walk about, cover a space

specchio.etymology: Continues Latin speculum ('mirror', from specere, 'to look at'), with syncope of unstressed u (speclu) and regular -cl- > -kkj-.

speciale.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin speciālem (accusative of speciālis, 'individual, particular, special'), derived from speciēs ('appearance, form, kind, sort').

spendere.etymology: Continues Latin expendĕre ('to weigh out money, pay out'), with apheresis of initial ex-, from pendĕre ('to weigh').

spento.etymology: Past participle and participial adjective of spegnere ('to extinguish, put out, turn off'), continuing Vulgar Latin *expinctum (from *expingĕre, 'to obliterate, efface, extinguish', formed from ex- + pingere 'to paint', with semantic influence from exstinguere 'to extinguish').

history.meaning: to extinguish -> extinguished, off, dull, lifeless

sperare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin spērāre ('to hope, look for, expect'), denominative verb built on the stem of spēs ('hope').

spesso.etymology: Continues Classical Latin spissum (accusative of spissus, 'thick, dense, compact, crowded, frequent'); the adverbial sense 'often, frequently' developed directly from the temporal sense 'closely packed in time, at short intervals'.

spiegare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin explicāre ('to unfold, unroll, spread out; to set forth, explain'), compound of ex- ('out') + plicāre ('to fold'), with regular evolution of initial ex- to s-, -pl- to -pi-, and voicing of intervocalic -c- to -g-.

history.meaning: to unfold, spread out; to explain

spingere.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *expingĕre ('to push out, thrust, drive away'), formed from ex- ('out') + the stem of impingere ('to drive against, thrust', from in- + pangere, 'to drive in, fasten').

history.meaning: to drive into, thrust against, push

spostare.etymology: Formed within Italian from the privative/separative prefix s- (< Latin ex-) + postare ('to place, station', derived from posto, 'place', < Latin positum), literally 'to move out of its place'.

history.meaning: place -> to station -> to move, shift, displace

spremuta.etymology: Substantivized feminine past participle of spremere ('to squeeze, press out'), which continues Vulgar Latin *expremĕre (recompounded from Classical Latin exprimere, from ex- + premere, 'to press'), designating freshly squeezed fruit juice.

spugna.etymology: Continues Latin spŏngĭa ('sea sponge'), borrowed from Greek σπογγιά (spongiá), with regular Tuscan palatalisation of -ngj- to /ɲɲ/.

squadra.etymology: Deverbal noun from squadrare ('to make square'), continuing Vulgar Latin *exquadrāre (from ex- + Classical Latin quadrāre, 'to make square', from quadrus, 'square', related to quattuor, 'four'); originally the mason's or carpenter's set-square, then a body of soldiers drawn up in a square formation, and hence any 'team, crew, squad'.

history.meaning: to square -> set-square; military squad; team

squillo.etymology: Deverbal noun from squillare ('to ring out, peal, blare'), derived from Old Italian squilla ('small bell, handbell'), a borrowing from Gothic *skilla or Lombardic skilla ('bell'; compare Old High German scella, 'little bell'), of imitative Germanic origin.

history.meaning: ring, peal, blast (of a trumpet or phone)

squisito.etymology: Continues Classical Latin exquīsītum (accusative of exquīsītus, 'carefully sought out, choice, refined, excellent'), past participle of exquīrere ('to search out thoroughly', from ex- + quaerere, 'to seek'), with evolution of initial ex- to s-.

history.meaning: to seek out -> choice, refined, exquisite

stagista.etymology: Formed in modern Italian from French stage ('training placement', ultimately related to Old French estage, 'dwelling, period of residence') plus the agentive suffix -ista.

stamattina.etymology: Univerbation of sta mattina ('this morning'), composed of the aphaeretic feminine demonstrative sta (< Old Italian esta < Classical Latin ista, feminine of iste, 'this') + mattina ('morning', < Latin [hōra] mātūtīna).

stanotte.etymology: Univerbation of sta notte ('this night'), composed of the aphaeretic feminine demonstrative sta (< Old Italian esta < Classical Latin ista, 'this') + notte ('night', < Classical Latin noctem).

stanza.etymology: Continues Medieval and Vulgar Latin stantia ('staying place, abode, dwelling, room'), formed as an abstract/collective noun from the present participle stem stant- of Classical Latin stāre ('to stand, stay, reside').

stare.etymology: Continues Latin stāre ('to stand, remain firm'), expanding in Italian to cover staying in a place, health/well-being (come stai?), and progressive constructions with the gerund.

stasera.etymology: Univerbation of sta sera ('this evening'), composed of the aphaeretic feminine demonstrative sta (< Old Italian esta < Classical Latin ista, 'this') + sera ('evening', < Late Latin [diēs] sēra, feminine of sērus, 'late').

stazione.etymology: From Latin statiōnem ('standing place, post, stopping point', from stāre), extended in the railway age to train and bus stations.

stella.etymology: Continues Classical Latin stēlla ('star'), from Proto-Italic *stērolā, a diminutive of Proto-Indo-European *h₂stḗr ('star').

stendere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin extendere ('to stretch out, spread out, extend'), compound of ex- ('out') + tendere ('to stretch'), with regular reduction of initial ext- to st-.

history.meaning: to stretch out, spread out, extend
to stretch out, spread, hang out (laundry), lay down

stesso.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *istĭpsum (accusative of *istĭpse, 'that very one, the same'), an emphatic compound pronoun formed from Classical Latin iste ('this, that') + ipse ('self, very'), with aphaeresis of initial i- and regular assimilation of -ps- to -ss-.

stoffa.etymology: Early Romance noun linked to Old French estoffe and Middle High German stouf / Old High German stopfōn ('to stuff, pad, equip with cloth').

storia.etymology: Continues Classical Latin historia ('narrative, account, history, inquiry'), borrowed from Ancient Greek historía (ἱστορία, 'inquiry, knowledge obtained by inquiry, written account', from hístōr, 'witness, judge, learned man'), with Tuscan aphaeresis of unstressed initial hi- before s + consonant.

storico.etymology: Continues Classical Latin historicum (accusative of historicus, 'of history, historical; historian'), borrowed from Ancient Greek historikós (ἱστορικός), with aphaeresis of initial hi- on the model of storia.

storta.etymology: Substantivized feminine of storto, the past participle of storcere ('to twist, wrench, sprain', continuing Vulgar Latin *extorcēre for Classical Latin extorquēre), denoting a sprain, a bend, or a bent-necked distillation vessel (retort).

storto.etymology: Past participle and participial adjective of storcere ('to twist, bend'), continuing Classical Latin extortum (accusative of extortus, past participle of extorquēre, 'to twist out, wrench', from ex- + torquēre, 'to twist'), with reduction of initial ext- to st-.

strada.etymology: Continues Late Latin [via] strāta ('paved road, layered highway'), feminine singular of strātus, the past participle of Classical Latin sternere ('to spread out, strew, pave'), showing intervocalic voicing of -t- to -d-.

strano.etymology: Continues Classical Latin extrāneum (accusative of extrāneus, 'external, foreign, strange, unfamiliar', derived from extrā, 'outside'), via Old Italian stranio with reduction of initial extr- to str- and absorption of the palatal glide after -n-.

strapazzato.etymology: Participial adjective from strapazzare ('to mistreat, handle roughly, overwork; to scramble [eggs]'), probably a parasynthetic derivative formed from the intensive prefix stra- (< Latin extrā-) + pazzo ('mad, reckless'), or an expressive alteration of strappare ('to tear, pull').

history.meaning: to handle roughly, beat -> overworked, battered; scrambled (of eggs)

strapparsi.etymology: Pronominal and reflexive form of strappare ('to tear, rip, yank, pull away'), borrowed from Gothic *strappan or Lombardic *strappōn ('to pull taut, yank, pluck'; compare German straff, 'taut, tight').

history.meaning: to tear, rip -> to tear oneself, pull a muscle, rip

stretto.etymology: Continues Classical Latin strictum (accusative of strictus, 'drawn tight, narrow, close, strict'), past participle of stringere ('to draw tight, bind, squeeze'), with regular assimilation of -ct- to -tt- and development of short ĭ to closed e.

stringere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin stringere ('to draw tight, bind, press together, squeeze'), from Proto-Indo-European *streyg- ('to stroke, rub, press').

strizzare.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *strictiāre ('to squeeze tightly, wring'), a frequentative/intensive verb built on Classical Latin strictus (past participle of stringere, 'to draw tight, squeeze').

history.meaning: to wring, squeeze; (strizzare l'occhio) to wink

studio.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin studium ('zeal, eagerness, application, study, pursuit'), related to studēre ('to be eager, apply oneself, study').

history.meaning: to apply oneself -> zeal, study, place of study

stupire.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *stupīre, a fourth-conjugation remodeling of Classical Latin stupēre ('to be stunned, benumbed, amazed, astonished').

history.meaning: to amaze, astonish; to be astonished

stupito.etymology: Participial adjective from stupire ('to amaze, be astonished'), continuing Vulgar Latin *stupīre (< Classical Latin stupēre, 'to be stunned, amazed').

su.etymology: Apocopated form of Old Italian suso ('up, above, upon'), which continues Late and Vulgar Latin sūsum (for Classical Latin sūrsum, 'upward, on high', contracted from *subvorsum, 'turned from below', from sub- + vertere).

subito.etymology: Continues Classical Latin subitō ('suddenly, unexpectedly, immediately'), the adverbial ablative of subitus ('sudden, unexpected', originally the past participle of subīre, 'to come up stealthily, approach suddenly', from sub- + īre, 'to go').

history.meaning: to come up suddenly -> sudden (adv. suddenly, at once)

sud.etymology: Borrowed from French sud ('south'), itself a maritime borrowing from Old English sūþ ('south'), from Proto-Germanic *sunþaz ('south, sunward side', related to *sunnǭ, 'sun').

sui.etymology: Articulated preposition formed by the fusion of the preposition su ('on, upon', < Late Latin sūsum) and the masculine plural definite article i (< Old Italian li < Latin illī).

sul.etymology: Articulated preposition formed by the fusion of the preposition su ('on, upon', < Late Latin sūsum) and the masculine singular definite article il (< Latin illum).

sulla.etymology: Articulated preposition formed by the fusion of the preposition su ('on, upon', < Late Latin sūsum) and the feminine singular definite article la (< Latin illam), with syntactic gemination of -l-.

sulle.etymology: Articulated preposition formed by the fusion of the preposition su ('on, upon', < Late Latin sūsum) and the feminine plural definite article le (< Latin illās), with syntactic gemination of -l-.

sullo.etymology: Articulated preposition formed by the fusion of the preposition su ('on, upon', < Late Latin sūsum) and the masculine singular definite article lo (< Latin illum), with syntactic gemination of -l-.

history.meaning: on + the -> on the (masculine singular before s + consonant, z, etc.)

suo.etymology: Continues Classical Latin suum (accusative of suus, 'his, her, its, their own'), from Old Latin sovos, from Proto-Indo-European *swós ('one's own', derived from the reflexive stem *swé).

suonare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin sonāre ('to sound, resound, make a noise, play an instrument'), derived from sonus ('sound'), with the Tuscan diphthong uo- generalized from stressed rhizotonic forms (such as suona < sŏnat) to the infinitive alongside the variant sonare.

history.meaning: to sound, resound, play an instrument

suono.etymology: Continues Classical Latin sonum (accusative of sonus, 'sound, noise, tone'), from Proto-Indo-European *swenh₂- ('to sound, resound'), with regular Tuscan diphthongization of stressed short open ŏ to uo in an open syllable.

superare.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin superāre ('to go over, rise above, surmount, surpass, overcome'), denominative verb from super ('above, over, beyond').

history.meaning: above, over -> to surmount, surpass, overcome

sveglia.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from svegliare ('to wake up, awaken', < Vulgar Latin *exvigilāre), denoting first the act of waking or military reveille and then an alarm clock.

history.meaning: to wake up -> awakening, reveille, alarm clock

svegliare.etymology: Formed with the intensive prefix s- (< Latin ex-) from vegliare ('to stay awake, watch', < Classical Latin vigilāre, via Old Provençal velhar or northern Italian palatalization of syncopated *viglāre), or directly continuing Vulgar Latin *exvigilāre ('to rouse from sleep, awaken').

svelto.etymology: Originated as the past participle of svellere ('to pluck out, uproot, tear away', < Vulgar Latin *exvellĕre, from ex- + Classical Latin vellere, 'to pluck, pull out'); from the literal sense 'pulled free, detached, unencumbered' evolved the figurative sense 'nimble, brisk, quick, agile'.

history.meaning: to uproot -> pulled free, unencumbered -> quick, nimble, brisk

svuotare.etymology: Formed within Italian from the privative/intensive prefix s- (< Latin ex-) + vuotare ('to empty', denominative from vuoto, 'empty', < Vulgar Latin *vŏcĭtus).

history.meaning: empty -> to empty -> to empty out completely, drain

sì.etymology: Continues Classical Latin sīc ('so, thus, in this manner'), used in Late and Vulgar Latin as an affirmative reply (as in sīc est, 'so it is'), with regular loss of final -c.

tablet.etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English tablet (ellipsis of tablet computer), itself borrowed from Old French tablete ('small flat slab, writing tablet'), diminutive of table (< Classical Latin tabula, 'board, plank, writing tablet').

taccuino.etymology: Continues Medieval Latin tacuinum (famous from the Tacuinum sanitatis, the 13th-century Latin translation of an 11th-century medical treatise by Ibn Buṭlān), borrowed from Arabic taqwīm (تَقْوِيم, 'proper arrangement, synoptic table, almanac, calendar', verbal noun of qawwama, 'to set straight, organize'); from 'almanac, pocket calendar' the meaning shifted to 'pocket notebook, notepad'.

tagliare.etymology: Continues Late Latin taliāre ('to split, cut, prune, cleave'), a denominative verb derived from Classical Latin tālea ('cutting, twig, graft, stake'), with regular palatalization of -lj- to -gli-.

talento.etymology: Continues Classical Latin talentum ('a Greek unit of weight and sum of money'), borrowed from Ancient Greek tálanton (τάλαντον, 'balance, scale, weight, monetary talent'); the modern sense 'natural aptitude, gift, ability' arose in Medieval Latin and Romance through figurative interpretation of the Parable of the Talents (Matthew 25:14–30).

history.meaning: monetary talent -> God-given endowment, natural aptitude

tallone.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *tālō, *tālōnem, augmentative of Classical Latin tālus ('anklebone, heel').

tanto.etymology: Continues Classical Latin tantum (accusative of tantus, 'of such size, so great, so much', and adverb tantum, 'so much, to such a degree').

history.meaning: so great, so much, to such a degree

tappeto.etymology: Continues Classical Latin tapētum (variant of tapēte, 'carpet, rug, tapestry, coverlet'), borrowed from Ancient Greek tápēs, tápētos (τάπης; diminutive tapḗtion, ταπήτιον, 'rug, carpet'), with expressive or Tuscan gemination of intervocalic -p-.

tardi.etymology: Continues Classical Latin tardē ('slowly, late', adverb of tardus, 'slow, tardy, late'), with final -e replaced by the characteristic Italian adverbial suffix -i (on the model of temporal adverbs like ieri and domani).

targhetta.etymology: Diminutive formed within Italian from targa ('shield, plaque, plate', borrowed from Franconian or Lombardic *targa, 'shield, buckler') + the diminutive suffix -etta, designating a small nameplate, doorplate, or label.

history.meaning: plaque, plate -> small nameplate, label, badge

tasca.etymology: Continues Medieval Latin tasca ('pouch, bag, pocket', attested in Italy from the 11th century), of disputed origin: either related to Old High German tasca ('bag, pouch', > German Tasche) or derived by metathesis from Medieval Latin taxa ('tax assessment, pouch for money').

tasto.etymology: Deverbal noun from tastare ('to touch, feel, probe'), which continues Vulgar Latin *taxitāre, an intensive/frequentative of Classical Latin taxāre ('to touch sharply, handle, feel, estimate'); from the general sense 'touch, feel' it specialized to denote the fret of a lute/viol and the key of a keyboard or push-button.

history.meaning: to touch, feel -> touch; key (of a piano/keyboard), button

tavolino.etymology: Diminutive of tavolo ('table', masculine back-formation from tavola, continuing Classical Latin tabula, 'board, plank, table') + the diminutive suffix -ino.

history.meaning: table -> small table, coffee table, desk

tavolo.etymology: Masculine back-formation from feminine tavola (< Latin tabula, 'plank, board, table'), distinguishing a piece of furniture (il tavolo) from the laid dining table (a tavola).

taxi.etymology: Internationalism borrowed from French taxi, a shortening of taximètre ('taximeter cab'), coined from French taxe ('tariff, fare', < Medieval Latin taxa) + Ancient Greek métron (μέτρον, 'measure').

tazza.etymology: Borrowed in the Middle Ages from Arabic ṭāsa (طَاسَة, 'shallow metal bowl, drinking cup'), itself a borrowing from Persian tāsa / Middle Persian tāšt ('bowl, goblet').

te.etymology: Continues Classical Latin tē (accusative and ablative singular of the second-person personal pronoun tū, 'you, thee'), from Proto-Indo-European *twé.

teiera.etymology: Formed from tè ('tea', ultimately from Min Nan Chinese tê via Dutch thee) + the vessel suffix -iera (< French -ière, modeled directly on French théière, 'teapot').

telefonata.etymology: Formed within Italian from telefonare ('to telephone', denominative from telefono) + the participial action-noun suffix -ata.

history.meaning: telephone -> to call by phone -> phone call

telefono.etymology: Adapted from French téléphone / English telephone, a neoclassical compound formed from Ancient Greek têle (τῆλε, 'far off, at a distance') + phōnḗ (φωνή, 'voice, sound').

history.meaning: apparatus for transmitting sound over a distance

telo.etymology: Masculine noun extracted within Italian from tela ('woven fabric, cloth, canvas', continuing Classical Latin tēla, 'web, warp, woven cloth', from *tex-lā, related to texere, 'to weave'), denoting a single width or sheet of cloth.

history.meaning: cloth, fabric -> sheet of cloth, towel, tarpaulin

tempesta.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *tempĕsta (for Classical tempĕstās, tempestātis, 'season, weather, storm'), derived from tĕmpus ('time, weather').

tempo.etymology: Continues Latin tempus ('time, season, weather condition'), which is why one Italian word naturally covers both clock time and the weather.

tenda.etymology: Continues Medieval and Vulgar Latin tenda ('tent, awning, curtain'), a deverbal noun from Classical Latin tendere ('to stretch, spread out', as in tabernāculum tendere, 'to pitch a tent'), originally denoting any stretched cloth.

history.meaning: to stretch, spread out, pitch (a tent)

tenere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin tenēre ('to hold, keep, grasp, maintain'), originally a stative verb from Proto-Indo-European *ten- ('to stretch, extend').

termosifone.etymology: Compound formed from the neoclassical prefix termo- (< Ancient Greek thermós, θερμός, 'hot, warm') + sifone ('siphon, pipe', < Classical Latin sīphō, sīphōnis < Ancient Greek sīphōn, σίφων, 'pipe, tube'), originally designating a thermal siphon water-circulation heating apparatus and by extension a domestic radiator.

terra.etymology: Continues Classical Latin terra ('dry land, earth, ground, soil, country'), from Proto-Italic *terzā (< Proto-Indo-European *ters-eh₂, 'dry place, dry land', from the root *ters-, 'to dry').

terracotta.etymology: Compound of terra ('earth, clay', Latin tĕrra) + cotta ('baked, fired', feminine past participle of cuocere < Latin cŏquĕre).

terribile.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin terribilem (accusative of terribilis, 'frightful, dreadful, terrible'), derived from terrēre ('to frighten, terrify').

terzo.etymology: Continues Classical Latin tertium (accusative of tertius, 'third', ordinal numeral derived from trēs, 'three', from Proto-Indo-European *tr̥tyós), with regular affrication of post-consonantal -tj- to -z- (/ts/).

testa.etymology: Continues Classical Latin testa ('earthenware pot, jug, tile, potsherd, shell'), which in Late and Vulgar Latin came to be used metaphorically and colloquially for the skull ('brain-pan') and ultimately displaced Classical Latin caput as the unmarked word for 'head'.

testardo.etymology: Formed from testa ('head', < Latin testa) + the pejorative/characterizing suffix -ardo (of Germanic origin, from Frankish *-hard, 'hard, bold', via Old French; compare French têtard), literally 'hard-headed'.

tetto.etymology: Continues Classical Latin tēctum ('roof, ceiling, shelter, house'), substantivized neuter past participle of tegere ('to cover', from Proto-Indo-European *(s)teg-, 'to cover'), with regular assimilation of -ct- to -tt-.

ti.etymology: Unstressed (clitic) second-person singular object pronoun continuing Classical Latin tē (accusative, 'you, thee') and tibī (dative, 'to you'), with regular raising of unstressed final -e to -i in protonic and enclitic positions.

tiepido.etymology: Continues Classical Latin tepidum (accusative of tepidus, 'lukewarm, mildly warm, tepid', related to tepēre, 'to be warm'), with Tuscan diphthongization of stressed short open ĕ to ie in an open proparoxytonic syllable (alongside the undiphthongized variant tepido).

tiglio.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *tilius for classical feminine tilia ('linden or lime tree'), prized across Italian courtyards and avenues (viali dei tigli) for its honey-scented June blossoms.

timbro.etymology: Borrowed from French timbre ('clapperless bell struck from outside; resonance, tone quality; crest above a shield; official stamp or postmark'), which continues Medieval Latin tympanum (< Ancient Greek týmpanon, τύμπανον, 'kettle-drum, tambourine').

history.meaning: bell, tone quality (timbre); crest, official stamp

tirare.etymology: Continues Late and Vulgar Latin *tīrāre ('to pull, draw, drag, throw'), a pan-Western-Romance verb of uncertain and much-debated origin (variously explained as an aphaeretic derivative of martyriāre 'to torture on the rack', a blend involving Latin trahere 'to draw', or a borrowing from a Germanic or pre-Latin root).

history.meaning: to pull, draw, throw, shoot, blow (of wind)

titolo.etymology: Continues Latin tĭtŭlus ('inscription, label, heading of a scroll or book').

toccare.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *toccāre ('to knock, strike lightly, tap a bell, touch'), formed from an expressive/onomatopoeic root *tokk- imitating a light knock or tap.

history.meaning: to touch, feel; to fall to (one's turn or duty)

togliere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin tollere ('to lift up, raise, take away, remove'), with palatalization of -ll- to -gli- generalized to the infinitive from palatalized present-stem forms (*tolliō > tolglio/tolgo, togli, toglie).

history.meaning: to lift up, take away, remove
to take away, remove, take off

tonalità.etymology: Formed from tonale ('tonal', derived from tono, 'tone, pitch') + the abstract noun suffix -ità (< Latin -itātem; compare French tonalité), denoting musical tonality or a shade/hue of color.

history.meaning: tone -> tonal -> tonality, key; shade, hue

tono.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin tonum (accusative of tonus, 'tension of a cord, pitch, tone, accent'; compare the inherited popular doublet tuono), borrowed from Ancient Greek tónos (τόνος, 'cord, tension, pitch, musical mode', from teínō, 'to stretch').

topolino.etymology: Diminutive of topo ('mouse, rat', continuing Late Latin talpum, masculine variant of Classical Latin talpa, 'mole', which shifted in Italian to 'mouse, rat') + the diminutive suffix -ino.

torcia.etymology: Borrowed from Old French torche ('twisted bundle of straw, torch'), which continues Vulgar Latin *torca (altered from Classical Latin torques / *torqua, 'twisted collar, wreath', from torquēre, 'to twist'), originally denoting a twisted rope of tow soaked in wax or resin.

tornare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin tornāre ('to turn on a lathe, round off', from tornus, 'lathe', < Ancient Greek tórnos, τόρνος, 'lathe, carpenter's compass'), which in Late and Vulgar Latin broadened in meaning to 'to turn around, turn back, return'.

history.meaning: lathe -> to turn on a lathe; (Late Latin) to turn around, return
to return, come back, go back

torta.etymology: From Late Latin tōrta (panis), originally a round 'twisted' or rolled loaf/pastry (related to torquēre, 'to twist').

tovaglia.etymology: Borrowed via Old French touaille or Old Provençal toalha from Franconian *thwahlja ('towel, cloth for drying after washing'; compare Old High German dwahila, derived from *thwahan, 'to wash'), which in Italian specialized to mean 'tablecloth'.

tovagliolo.etymology: Diminutive formed within Italian from tovaglia ('tablecloth', ultimately from Franconian *thwahlja, 'towel, linen cloth') + the diminutive suffix -olo (< Latin -olum), designating a small table linen or napkin.

tra.etymology: Continues Classical Latin intrā ('inside, within, between, among'), with aphaeresis of initial unstressed in- in proclitic prepositional position (compare the doublet fra < infrā).

traffico.etymology: Deverbal noun from trafficare ('to trade, carry on commerce; to bustle about'), attested in Italian commercial usage since the 14th century and of uncertain origin (possibly from Vulgar Latin *transficāre, 'to shift goods across', or from Catalan trafegar / Arabic tafrīq, 'distribution'); the modern sense 'road traffic, movement of vehicles' was reinforced by English traffic.

history.meaning: to trade, deal in goods -> trade, commerce
commerce, trade; street traffic, circulation of vehicles

tralcio.etymology: Continues Classical Latin trāducem (accusative of trādux, trāducis, 'vine-branch trained across from tree to tree, vine-shoot', derived from trādūcere, 'to lead across'), via a syncopated Vulgar Latin form *tralce remodeled in the suffix.

tranne.etymology: Univerbation of the imperative phrase tra'ne ('take away from it!', hence 'except, save for'), composed of tra' (apocopated second-person singular imperative of trarre, 'to draw, take out', < Classical Latin trahere) + the enclitic pronominal particle ne ('from it, thereof', < Latin inde), with syntactic gemination of -n-.

tranquillo.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin tranquillum (accusative of tranquillus, 'calm, still, quiet, peaceful', compounded from trāns- + *-quillus, from the Proto-Indo-European root *kʷyeh₁- of quiēs, 'rest, quiet').

trappola.etymology: Diminutive derivative of Medieval Latin trappa ('trap, snare, pitfall'), itself borrowed from Franconian or Lombardic *trappa ('trap, snare').

trasformare.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin trānsformāre ('to change in shape, transform, metamorphose'), compound of trāns- ('across, beyond') + formāre ('to form, shape', from forma, 'form, shape').

trasformazione.etymology: Learned continuation of Late Latin trānsformātiōnem (accusative of trānsformātiō, 'change of shape, transformation'), action noun derived from Classical Latin trānsformāre ('to transform').

history.meaning: to transform -> transformation, change of form

trasloco.etymology: Deverbal noun from traslocare ('to move house, relocate, transfer'), a compound formed from tras- (< Latin trāns-, 'across, from one place to another') + locare ('to place, locate', < Classical Latin locāre, from locus, 'place').

history.meaning: to relocate, move house -> move, removal, relocation

trave.etymology: Continues Classical Latin trabem (accusative of trabs, 'beam, timber, rafter'), from Proto-Indo-European *treb- ('dwelling, beam, timber'), with regular spirantization of intervocalic -b- to -v-.

tre.etymology: Continues Classical Latin trēs (masculine/feminine) and tria (neuter, 'three'), from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes ('three').

tremare.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *tremāre, a first-conjugation remodeling of Classical Latin tremere ('to tremble, shake, quake, quiver'), from Proto-Indo-European *trem- ('to tremble').

trenino.etymology: Diminutive formed within Italian from treno ('train', borrowed from French train in the railway sense after English train, ultimately from Old French trainer, 'to draw, drag', < Vulgar Latin *tragīnāre from trahere) + the diminutive suffix -ino.

history.meaning: line of pulled carriages, railway train
train -> little train, toy train, narrow-gauge train

treno.etymology: In its railway sense, adapted in the nineteenth century from French train and English train (ultimately from Old French traïner, 'to draw, pull along').

trenta.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *trēnta, contracted from Classical Latin trīgintā ('thirty', derived from trēs, 'three').

trentacinque.etymology: Compound numeral formed within Italian from trenta ('thirty', < Vulgar Latin *trēnta < Classical trīgintā) + cinque ('five', < Vulgar Latin *cīnque < Classical quīnque).

trentotto.etymology: Compound numeral formed within Italian from trenta ('thirty', with regular elision of final -a before a vowel) + otto ('eight', < Classical Latin octō).

triste.etymology: Continues Classical Latin trīstem (accusative of trīstis, 'sad, sorrowful, mournful, gloomy, bitter').

troppo.etymology: Originated as the noun troppo ('herd, flock, crowd, multitude'), borrowed via Medieval Latin troppus from Franconian *throp ('assembly, cluster, village'; compare French troupe and trop); in quantitative constructions ('a crowd of, an excess of') it grammaticalized into an adjective and adverb meaning 'too much, excessive, too'.

trovare.etymology: Continues Late and Vulgar Latin *tropāre ('to compose a liturgical trope or melody, invent, discover, find', derived from Late Latin tropus, 'rhetorical figure, song, trope', < Ancient Greek trópos, τρόπος, 'turn, manner, melodic mode'), spread across Romance partly through Old Provençal trobar ('to compose verse, find').

history.meaning: rhetorical/melodic figure -> to invent, compose, find

tu.etymology: Continues Latin tū, the inherited Indo-European singular second-person subject pronoun.

tubo.etymology: Learned borrowing from Classical Latin tubus ('pipe, water-pipe, tube').

tuo.etymology: Continues Classical Latin tuum (accusative of tuus, 'thy, your [singular]'), from Old Latin tovos, from Proto-Indo-European *twós (possessive adjective built on the second-person singular pronoun *túh₂, 'thou').

tutela.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin tūtēla ('watching, keeping, safeguard, protection, legal guardianship'), derived from tūtārī ('to watch over, guard, protect', frequentative of tuērī, 'to look after, protect').

history.meaning: to watch over, guard -> protection, guardianship

tutto.etymology: Continues Late and Vulgar Latin *tōttum / *tūttum, an expressive geminated variant of Classical Latin tōtum (accusative of tōtus, 'whole, entire, all', probably remodeled under the influence of cūnctus or nullus).

tè.etymology: Borrowed via Dutch/French thé from Hokkien (Min Nan) Chinese tê, reflecting maritime trade from Xiamen/Fujian.

uccello.etymology: Continues Late and Vulgar Latin aucellum (accusative of aucellus, 'bird', syncopated from *avicellus, diminutive of Classical Latin avis, 'bird'), with the palatal sibilant and initial u- influenced by Old French oisel / Old Provençal auzel.

uff.etymology: Onomatopoeic interjection imitating a puff of breath or sigh of impatience, annoyance, weariness, heat, or relief.

history.meaning: ugh, phew (interjection of impatience, boredom, or weariness)

uffa.etymology: Expressive Italian expansion of the onomatopoeic interjection uff, imitating a puff of breath to express annoyance, boredom, or impatience.

history.meaning: ugh, oh bother (interjection of annoyance or boredom)

ufficiale.etymology: Semi-learned continuation of Late Latin officiālem (accusative of officiālis, 'pertaining to duty or office; magistrate's attendant, official', derived from Classical Latin officium, 'duty, service, office'), with labial raising of unstressed initial o- to u-.

ufficialmente.etymology: Formed within Italian from the adjective ufficiale ('official', < Late Latin officiālis) + the adverbial suffix -mente (< Classical Latin ablative mente, 'in an [official] manner').

ufficio.etymology: Semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin officium ('service, kindness, duty, function, office', contracted from *opificium, from opus, 'work' + facere, 'to do, make'), with Tuscan labial raising of pretonic initial o- to u- before -f-.

uguale.etymology: Continues Classical Latin aequālem (accusative of aequālis, 'level, even, equal, like', derived from aequus, 'even, level, fair'), via eguale with labial assimilation of initial unstressed e- to u- before the labiovelar cluster -gu-.

ultimo.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin ultimum (accusative of ultimus, 'farthest, most distant, last, final'), superlative adjective formed from the archaic preposition uls ('beyond'; compare ultrā, 'beyond', and ulterior, 'farther').

umido.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin ūmidum / hūmidum (accusative of ūmidus, 'moist, damp, wet, humid', related to ūmēre, 'to be moist, be wet', and ūmor, 'moisture').

undici.etymology: Continues Classical Latin ūndecim ('eleven'), a compound numeral formed from ūnus ('one') + decem ('ten').

uniforme.etymology: Learned continuation of Late Latin ūnifōrmem (accusative of ūnifōrmis, 'having only one shape, uniform', compounded from ūnus, 'one' + forma, 'form, shape'); the substantive sense 'military or institutional uniform' was reinforced by French (habit) uniforme.

unire.etymology: Continues Classical Latin ūnīre ('to join together, unite, make into one'), denominative verb derived from ūnus ('one').

history.meaning: one -> to make one, join, unite

uno.etymology: Continues Classical Latin ūnum (accusative of ūnus, 'one, single, alone'), from Old Latin oinos, from Proto-Indo-European *óynos ('one, single').

uomo.etymology: Continues Classical Latin homō ('human being, man', related to humus, 'earth, soil', from Proto-Indo-European *dʰǵʰm̥mō, 'earthling'), with regular Tuscan diphthongization of stressed short open ŏ to uo in an open syllable (while the plural uomini continues the oblique stem hominēs).

uovo.etymology: Continues Latin ovum ('egg'), preserving the Latin neuter plural ending -a in its feminine Italian plural le uova.

usare.etymology: Continues Late and Vulgar Latin ūsāre ('to use, make use of, practice, be accustomed to'), a frequentative verb built on the past participle stem ūs- (ūsus) of Classical Latin ūtī ('to use').

history.meaning: to use regularly, be accustomed to
to use, employ, wear, be accustomed to

uscire.etymology: Continues Classical Latin exīre ('to go out, come forth, exit', compound of ex- 'out' + īre 'to go'), via Old Italian escire with alteration of unstressed initial e- to u- under the lexical and phonetic influence of uscio ('door, exit', < Late Latin ūstium for Classical ōstium); rhizotonic forms like esco and esce retain the original vowel.

history.meaning: to go out, exit, come out, leave

utile.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin ūtilem (accusative of ūtilis, 'useful, serviceable, beneficial, profitable'), derived from ūtī ('to use').

valigia.etymology: Attested in medieval Italian (valigia) and borrowed into French as valise; of debated Late Latin or Arabic origin, naming a rider's or traveller's bag.

valvola.etymology: Learned scientific and technical borrowing from Modern Latin valvula ('seed-pod shell, anatomical valve, mechanical valve'), diminutive of Classical Latin valva (usually plural valvae, 'leaves of a folding double door').

history.meaning: small folding flap, anatomical or mechanical valve

valzer.etymology: 19th-century loanword from German Walzer ('waltz'), agent noun from walzen ('to revolve, glide in circles').

vasetto.etymology: Diminutive formed within Italian from vaso ('vessel, pot, jar, vase', continuing Classical Latin vāsum / vās) + the diminutive suffix -etto.

vaso.etymology: Continues Latin vāsum (collateral masculine form of neuter vās, 'vessel, container, pot').

vassoio.etymology: Continues Late Latin missōrĭum / *vassōrĭum (crossed with vas, 'vessel, dish'), originally a flat wooden winnowing or serving tray.

vecchio.etymology: Continues Late and Vulgar Latin veclum (attested in the Appendix Probi as vetulus non veclus), syncopated from Classical Latin vetulum (accusative of vetulus, 'little old one, old', diminutive of vetus, veteris, 'old, aged'), with regular evolution of post-vocalic -cl- to -cchi-.

vedere.etymology: Continues Latin vidēre ('to see'), with regular lowering of short Latin i to closed e in vedere.

velo.etymology: Continues Classical Latin vēlum ('sail, curtain, awning, cloth covering, veil').

veloce.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin vēlōcem (accusative of vēlōx, vēlōcis, 'swift, fleet, rapid, quick').

velocità.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin vēlōcitātem (accusative of vēlōcitās, 'swiftness, fleetness, speed, rapidity', derived from vēlōx, 'swift'), with apocope of the final syllable after the stressed vowel.

venatura.etymology: Formed from venare ('to mark with veins', from vena, 'vein, streak in wood or marble', < Classical Latin vēna) + the suffix -tura (or directly continuing Late Latin vēnātūra), denoting the grain of wood or veining in stone, leaves, or wings.

vendere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin vēndere ('to sell, offer for sale'), contracted in early Latin from the phrase vēnum dare ('to put up for sale', from vēnum, accusative of *vēnus, 'sale, purchase price', < Proto-Indo-European *wes-no-, + dare, 'to give').

vendita.etymology: Continues Medieval and Vulgar Latin *vēndita ('sale'), substantivized feminine past participle built on vēndere ('to sell', replacing Classical Latin vēnditiō) on the analogy of perdita ('loss') and reddita ('return, yield').

venerdì.etymology: Continues Latin Veneris diēs ('day of Venus'), preserving the ancient planetary week in everyday speech.

venire.etymology: Continues Latin venīre ('to come'), preserving palatalized velar forms like vengo (< veniō) alongside diphthongized viene (< venit).

venti.etymology: Continues Classical Latin vīgintī ('twenty', from Proto-Indo-European *(d)wīdḱm̥ti, 'two tens'), via contracted Vulgar Latin *vīnti.

venticinque.etymology: Compound numeral formed within Italian from venti ('twenty', < Classical Latin vīgintī) + cinque ('five', < Vulgar Latin *cīnque < Classical quīnque).

ventilatore.etymology: Learned adaptation of Classical Latin ventilātor, ventilātōris ('winnower, one who tosses grain in the wind', agent noun from ventilāre, 'to fan, air, winnow', derived from ventus, 'wind'), repurposed in modern technical usage (after French ventilateur and English ventilator) to denote a mechanical fan.

ventinove.etymology: Compound numeral formed within Italian from venti ('twenty', < Classical Latin vīgintī) + nove ('nine', < Classical Latin novem).

ventiquattro.etymology: Compound numeral formed within Italian from venti ('twenty', < Classical Latin vīgintī) + quattro ('four', < Classical Latin quattuor).

vento.etymology: Continues Classical Latin ventum (accusative of ventus, 'wind'), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wéh₁ntos ('wind', originally a participial derivative of the root *h₂weh₁-, 'to blow').

ventotto.etymology: Compound numeral formed within Italian from venti ('twenty', with regular elision of final -i before a vowel) + otto ('eight', < Classical Latin octō).

veramente.etymology: Formed within Italian from the feminine adjective vera ('true', from Latin vēra) plus the adverbial suffix -mente (originally Latin ablative mente, 'with a ... mind').

verde.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *virdem (attested in the Appendix Probi as viridis non virdis), syncopated from Classical Latin viridem (accusative of viridis, 'green, fresh, blooming, vigorous', derived from virēre, 'to be green, flourish').

history.meaning: to be green -> green, fresh, blooming

verdura.etymology: Formed from verde ('green', < Vulgar Latin virdis < Classical viridis) + the abstract/collective noun suffix -ura (< Late Latin -ūra), denoting first 'greenness, greenery, foliage' and then collectively 'green vegetables, greens'.

verità.etymology: Continues Classical Latin vēritātem (accusative of vēritās, 'truth, reality, truthfulness', abstract noun derived from vērus, 'true'), via Old Italian veritade with apocope of the final syllable.

vernice.etymology: Continues Medieval Latin veronix, vernicis ('sandarac resin, crystalline resin, varnish'), borrowed from Byzantine Greek beroníkē / bereníkē (βερονίκη / βερενίκη), derived from the name of the ancient Cyrenaican port city of Berenīcē (Βερενίκη, modern Benghazi in Libya), from which amber-colored resins and varnishes were imported.

vero.etymology: Continues Classical Latin vērum (accusative of vērus, 'true, real, genuine'), from Proto-Indo-European *weh₁-ro- ('true, trustworthy').

versare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin versāre ('to turn often, twist, overturn, tilt', frequentative of vertere, 'to turn'), which in Late and Vulgar Latin developed the specific meaning 'to tilt a vessel, pour out, spill'.

history.meaning: to turn -> to turn over, tilt
to tilt a container, pour out, spill

verso.etymology: As a preposition ('toward, in the direction of, around'), continues Classical Latin versus ('turned toward, facing, toward', originally the past participle of vertere, 'to turn'); as a noun ('verse, line of poetry; birdcall, cry; direction'), continues Classical Latin versum (accusative of versus, 'furrow, turning of the plough, line of writing, verse', also from vertere).

history.meaning: to turn -> turned toward (prep); furrow, line of verse (noun)

verticale.etymology: Learned continuation of Late Latin verticālem (accusative of verticālis, 'directly overhead, at the zenith, vertical'), derived from Classical Latin vertex, verticis ('whirlpool, crown of the head, summit, zenith, pole', from vertere, 'to turn').

history.meaning: crown of the head, highest point, zenith

vestito.etymology: Continues Classical Latin vestītum (both the past participle of vestīre, 'to clothe, dress', and the fourth-declension noun vestītus, 'clothing, apparel, dress', derived from vestis, 'garment, clothing').

vetrato.etymology: Participial adjective formed from vetro ('glass', < Classical Latin vitrum) + the suffix -ato (< Latin -ātus; compare Medieval Latin vitrātus), meaning 'fitted or enclosed with glass panes, glazed'.

vetro.etymology: Continues Classical Latin vitrum ('glass'), with regular development of stressed short ĭ to closed e.

vi.etymology: Continues Classical Latin ibī ('there, in that place'), via aphaeretic Vulgar Latin *(i)bi with spirantization of -b- to v-; from its locative adverbial function ('there') it was also grammaticalized as the unstressed second-person plural object and reflexive pronoun ('you, to you', parallel to ci < ecce hīc for the first person plural and reinforced by unstressed vōs).

history.meaning: you, to you, yourselves (2pl clitic pronoun); there (locative clitic)

via.etymology: Continues Latin via ('road, way, street') unchanged in spelling; also used adverbially ('away, off') from phrases like andare per via.

viaggio.etymology: Borrowed from Old Provençal viatge (or Old French voiage), which continues Classical Latin viāticum ('provisions for a journey, travel money; journey', substantivized neuter of viāticus, derived from via, 'road, way'), with regular Gallo-Romance development of -ticum to -tge (adapted in Italian as -ggio).

viale.etymology: Substantivized masculine form of the adjective viale ('pertaining to a road or way'), continuing Late Latin viālem (accusative of viālis, derived from Classical Latin via, 'road, street, way').

vibrazione.etymology: Learned continuation of Late Latin vibrātiōnem (accusative of vibrātiō, 'shaking, brandishing, quivering'), action noun derived from Classical Latin vibrāre ('to shake, brandish, quiver, vibrate').

vicino.etymology: Continues Classical Latin vīcīnum (accusative of vīcīnus, 'near, neighboring; neighbor'), derived from vīcus ('row of houses, street, quarter, village', from Proto-Indo-European *weyḱ-, 'clan, settlement').

vicolo.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin vīculum (accusative of vīculus, 'small village, hamlet; narrow street, lane, alley'), diminutive of vīcus ('row of houses, street, quarter, village').

history.meaning: street, quarter -> narrow street, lane, alley

visita.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from visitare ('to go to see, visit'), which continues Classical Latin vīsitāre ('to go to see often, visit', frequentative of vīsere, 'to look at, go to see', itself an intensive of vidēre, 'to see').

history.meaning: to see -> to go to see -> to visit
to visit -> visit, call, medical examination

vista.etymology: Substantivized feminine past participle continuing Vulgar Latin *vīsta ('sight, view', formed from a remodeled past participle *vīstus of Classical Latin vidēre, 'to see', replacing Classical vīsa).

vita.etymology: Continues Classical Latin vīta ('life, way of life, existence'), derived from Proto-Indo-European *gʷih₃-wó-tā (from the root *gʷeyh₃-, 'to live'; compare vīvus and vīvere).

vite.etymology: Continues Classical Latin vītem (accusative of vītis, 'grapevine, creeping plant', from Proto-Indo-European *weh₁y-ti-, 'twining plant', from *weh₁y-, 'to twist, wind, plait'); the mechanical sense 'screw' developed within Italian as a metaphorical extension comparing the helical thread of a press screw to the spiral tendrils of a vine.

history.meaning: grapevine; screw (by analogy with spiral tendrils)

vivace.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin vīvācem (accusative of vīvāx, vīvācis, 'tenacious of life, long-lived, lively, vigorous, brisk'), derived from vīvere ('to live').

history.meaning: to live -> lively, vigorous, full of life

vivere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin vīvere ('to live, be alive, subsist, dwell'), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷíh₃weti (from the root *gʷeyh₃-, 'to live').

vivo.etymology: Continues Classical Latin vīvum (accusative of vīvus, 'alive, living, lively'), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷih₃wós ('alive', from the root *gʷeyh₃-, 'to live').

vocale.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin vōcālem (accusative of vōcālis, 'uttering a voice, sonorous, vocal'; as a feminine noun [littera] vōcālis, 'vowel', calqued on Ancient Greek [grámma] phōnêen), derived from vōx, vōcis ('voice').

voce.etymology: Continues Classical Latin vōcem (accusative of vōx, 'voice, sound, call, word, utterance'), from Proto-Indo-European *wṓkʷs ('voice', root noun from *wekʷ-, 'to speak, utter').

voi.etymology: Continues Classical Latin vōs (nominative and accusative plural of the second-person personal pronoun, 'you'), from Proto-Indo-European *wós, with regular vocalization of final -s to -i in monosyllables.

volentieri.etymology: Borrowed from Old French volentiers ('willingly, gladly'), which continues Late/Vulgar Latin *voluntāriīs / Classical Latin voluntāriē (adverb of voluntārius, 'willing, of one's own free will', from voluntās, 'will'), remodeled in its stem after the present participle volēns, volentis of velle ('to wish, want').

volere.etymology: Continues reconstructed Vulgar Latin *volēre, regularized from classical Latin velle ('to wish, want') on analogy with present forms like volō.

volta.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *vŏlta ('a turn, turning'), substantivized feminine of *vŏltus (remodeled past participle replacing Classical Latin volūtus of volvere, 'to roll, turn, revolve'), developing both the architectural sense 'vault, arched ceiling' (from the turning of an arch) and the temporal sense 'turn, time, occasion'.

vostro.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin vŏstrum (accusative of vŏster, an archaic and colloquial Latin variant of Classical vester, 'your [plural]', with the root vowel o maintained or restored by analogy with nŏster, 'our', and vōs, 'you').

voto.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin vōtum ('solemn promise to a deity, vow, wish, prayer', substantivized neuter past participle of vovēre, 'to vow, promise solemnly'); in modern usage extended to 'vote, suffrage' and 'academic mark, grade'.

history.meaning: to vow -> solemn vow, wish, offering
vow; vote, ballot; school grade, mark

vuoto.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *vŏcĭtum (accusative of *vŏcĭtus, 'empty, unoccupied', a participial adjective built on *vocāre, an old variant of Classical Latin vacāre, 'to be empty, be void'), via syncopated *vŏctu with assimilation of -ct- to -t- after the Tuscan diphthong uo (compare the literary doublet voto).

zecca.etymology: Represents two homographic words of distinct origin: (1) 'mint (place where coins are struck)', borrowed from Arabic sikka (سِكَّة, 'iron die for striking coins, coin, minthouse', as in dār al-sikka; source of idioms like nuovo di zecca, 'brand-new, mint-fresh'); (2) 'tick (parasitic arachnid)', borrowed from Lombardic *zecka ('tick'; compare Middle High German zëcke and English tick).

zero.etymology: Contracted from Old Italian zefiro / zevero, borrowed from Medieval Latin zephirum (introduced by the Pisan mathematician Leonardo Fibonacci in his Liber Abaci of 1202), an adaptation of Arabic ṣifr (صِفْر, 'empty, cipher, zero'; compare cifra), itself a semantic calque of Sanskrit śūnya (शून्य, 'empty, void, zero').

zia.etymology: Continues Late Latin thĭa ('aunt'), borrowed from Byzantine Greek θεία (theía, feminine of θεῖος, 'uncle').

zio.etymology: Continues Late Latin thīum (accusative of thīus, 'uncle'), borrowed from Ancient Greek theîos (θεῖος, 'uncle', originally the adjective 'divine, revered', adopted in Hellenistic and Byzantine Greek as a respectful kinship term).

zucchero.etymology: Borrowed in medieval maritime Italy from Arabic sukkar ('sugar'), ultimately from Sanskrit śarkarā ('gravel, grit, crystal sugar').

zuppa.etymology: Borrowed from Gothic *suppa or Lombardic *zuppa ('sop, slice of bread soaked in broth or liquid'; compare Old High German sopfa, related to Proto-Germanic *sūpaną, 'to sip, sup'), which shifted metonymically from the soaked bread to the soup poured over it.

history.meaning: slice of bread soaked in broth, sop
soup (especially thick soup served with bread)
